doc_description: Form 10-K for MGM Resorts International (FY2018) covering its U.S. and Macau integrated resorts, the distinctive MGP UPREIT master-lease structure with substantial fixed rent, the openings of MGM Cotai and MGM Springfield, post-year Empire City and Northfield/MGP transactions and Park MGM renovation financing, the launch of the MGM 2020 efficiency program and ROAR Digital JV, sizable share repurchases/dividends, and key risks/legal matters including mediation of the Oct. 1, 2017 Las Vegas shooting litigation and Macau concession renewal uncertainty.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Document type and period: Form 10-K annual report for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2018, filed by MGM Resorts International (Commission File No. 001-10362).
- Registrant details: Delaware corporation; EIN 88-0215232; principal executive offices at 3600 Las Vegas Boulevard South, Las Vegas, NV 89109; phone (702) 693-7120.
- Securities information: Common Stock, $0.01 par value, listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Shares outstanding as of February 22, 2019: 536,916,609. Aggregate market value of non-affiliate common stock as of June 30, 2018: $15.6 billion.
- Filing status: Well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; compliant with Exchange Act reporting and Interactive Data File submissions; not a shell company.
- Incorporated by reference: Portions of the definitive Proxy Statement for the 2018 Annual Meeting of Stockholders are incorporated into Part III.
- Table of contents highlights: Standard 10-K sections including Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Market for Equity and Issuer Purchases, Selected Financial Data, MD&A, Market Risk, Financial Statements and Notes, Controls and Procedures, and governance and compensation items.
- Business overview: MGM Resorts operates integrated casino, hotel, and entertainment resorts in the U.S. and Macau; MGM China Holdings Limited and MGM Growth Properties LLC (MGP) are key affiliates/subsidiaries referenced.
- MGP structure and master lease: MGP is a consolidated subsidiary organized as an UPREIT; its assets and businesses are conducted through MGM Growth Properties Operating Partnership LP. Under a master lease, a Company subsidiary (tenant) leases the real estate of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM (formerly Monte Carlo), Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor from an MGP subsidiary (landlord).
- Strategy: Ongoing reinvestment in resort assets to maintain competitive advantages through room remodels, restaurants, entertainment, nightlife, and amenities.
- Key business developments:
  - 2016: Acquisition of Boyd Gaming’s interest in Borgata; subsequently MGP acquired Borgata’s real property. Opening of MGM National Harbor; in 2017 MGP acquired its long-term leasehold interest and real property.
  - 2018: Openings of MGM Cotai (February) and MGM Springfield (August).
  - July 2018: MGP acquired Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park (Northfield) for about $1.1 billion; Hard Rock affiliate continues as manager.
  - September 2018: Agreement for MGM Resorts to acquire Northfield operating assets (Northfield OpCo) from MGP for about $275 million; to be added to the master lease; expected to close in first half of 2019.
  - December 2018: Agreement with MGP for approximately $638 million consideration related to Park MGM and NoMad Las Vegas renovations, with an amendment to the master lease; expected to close in Q1 2019.
  - January 2019: Completion of the acquisition of Empire City Casino’s real property and operations (Empire City) for approximately $864 million, subject to adjustments; subsequently, MGP acquired Empire City’s real property (sentence truncated in excerpt).

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: MGM Resorts International is referred to as the “Company,” “MGM Resorts,” or the “Registrant,” and together with its subsidiaries may also be referred to as “we,” “us” or “our.”
structure.summary:
- Company and structure: MGM Resorts International is a Delaware holding company that owns and operates integrated casino, hotel, and entertainment resorts in the U.S. and Macau. MGM Growth Properties (MGP) is a consolidated UPREIT subsidiary; its Operating Partnership owns real estate that is master-leased to an MGM subsidiary. MGM China (≈56% owned) operates in Macau through MGM Grand Paradise.
- Portfolio and reinvestment: The Company emphasizes continual capital investment to maintain premier resort positioning across markets.
- Major developments (2016–early 2019): Acquired Boyd’s interest in Borgata (2016) then sold Borgata real estate to MGP; opened MGM National Harbor (2016), MGM Cotai (Feb 2018), and MGM Springfield (Aug 2018). MGP acquired Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park (2018); MGM agreed to acquire Northfield operating assets from MGP and add them to the master lease. Entered a Park MGM lease transaction with MGP (~$638M consideration). Acquired Empire City (Jan 2019), then sold its real estate to MGP with leaseback and granted MGP a ROFO on certain adjacent land.
- Operations: Revenue is largely cash-based; results are not strictly seasonal but can vary with conventions, holidays, and high-end play. Resorts operate 24/7 (Empire City operates 20 hours daily). MGM operates primary casino and hotel functions; some amenities are managed or leased to third parties for brand/expertise.
- Segments and properties: 
  - Las Vegas Strip Resorts include Bellagio, MGM Grand Las Vegas (incl. The Signature), Mandalay Bay (incl. Delano and Four Seasons), The Mirage, Luxor, New York-New York (incl. The Park), Excalibur, Park MGM (incl. NoMad), and Circus Circus.
  - Regional Operations include MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Gold Strike Tunica, Borgata, MGM National Harbor, and MGM Springfield.
  - MGM China operates MGM Macau and MGM Cotai.
  - Also references CityCenter (50% owned, managed by MGM) and MGP’s Northfield (managed by Hard Rock).
  - As of year-end 2018, the consolidated portfolio comprises roughly 49,000 guestrooms, ~2.54 million square feet of casino space, ~31,600 slots, and ~2,050 tables.
- Revenue mix and gaming: Over half of domestic net revenue is from non-gaming (rooms, F&B, entertainment, other amenities). Casino offerings include slots, table games, race and sports books, and high-limit areas.
- Macau specifics: MGM China’s revenues are primarily gaming; the MGM Grand Paradise subconcession (granted by SJM) expires in 2020. Market segments are VIP (often via gaming promoters with commission/comp allowances) and main floor (higher margin, significant growth focus). Competition includes Macau concessionaires/subconcessionaires and regional/global gaming hubs.
- Competition and customers: Competes with U.S. and international gaming/hospitality operators and non-gaming destinations. Strategies include prime locations, high-quality facilities, top talent and service, unique entertainment, and differentiated marketing/loyalty.
- Marketing and loyalty: Multi-channel advertising, data-driven direct marketing, and loyalty programs (M life Rewards across gaming/non-gaming; Golden Lion Club in Macau) to increase visitation and spend.
- Strategy: Objectives center on operational enhancements, financial strength, corporate social responsibility (CSR), targeted geographic expansion, and business model innovation.
- Technology: Emphasis on cloud-first solutions, analytics, and eCommerce to drive efficiency and personalized guest experiences.
- People and development: Significant investment in recruiting, training, leadership development (e.g., MGM Resorts University).
- CSR and sustainability: Four pillars—diversity and inclusion; investing in community; caring for one another (philanthropy, volunteering); environmental sustainability. Numerous recognitions (Green Key, LEED Gold at select properties). CityCenter cited as a large-scale sustainable development; MGM China recognized in sustainability benchmarks.
- Growth and brand leverage: Balanced capital allocation across existing assets, development, and returns. Evaluates domestic/international expansion, sports/interactive and online gaming. Formed Roar Digital LLC with GVC (50/50 JV; initial $100M each) for U.S. sports betting and online gaming, leveraging MGM assets (subject to regulatory approvals).
- Intellectual property: Extensive U.S. and international trademarks for key resort brands; ongoing protection and enforcement.
- Workforce and labor relations: As of 12/31/2018, ~72,000 domestic employees (55k full-time, 17k part-time), plus ~11,000 at MGM China; ~39,000 covered by CBAs with several negotiations scheduled in 2019 across Las Vegas and regional properties. Recent acquisitions add unionized employees.
- Regulation: Operations subject to extensive gaming regulation and a broad array of business, AML, advertising, accessibility, zoning/building, and environmental laws; changes could affect operations and results.
- Forward-looking statements and risks: Cautions on uncertainties and a detailed risk summary, including leverage and rent obligations to MGP; market/credit conditions; covenants; competition; regulation; macroeconomic exposure; Macau concession renewal risk in 2020; reliance on Macau promoters; tax matters; weather/climate; concentration on the Las Vegas Strip; credit losses; impairments; geopolitical/travel risks; JV and development risks; insurance limitations; IP protection; anti-corruption compliance; litigation; labor relations; energy prices; cybersecurity/data privacy; CSR-related reputation; expansion/divestiture execution; gaming tax increases; and potential director/officer conflicts with MGM China.
- Leadership: Lists executive officers as of Feb 27, 2019 and notes changes effective March 1, 2019 (CFO resignation; Sanders appointed CFO/Treasurer; Hornbuckle appointed President/COO).
- Investor information: SEC filings available via company website and EDGAR; website also used to post MGM China information due to time zone differences.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
You should
 be aware that the occurrence of any of the events described in this section and elsewhere in this report or in any other of our filings with the SECcould
 have a material adverse effect on our business, financial position, results of operations and cash flows.
structure.summary:
- Document section: Item 1A. Risk Factors from an SEC filing, outlining material risks that could adversely affect the company’s business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows.

- Capital structure and liquidity
  - High leverage and significant debt maturities, exposure to rising interest rates, and dependence on access to capital markets and revolving credit capacity.
  - Restrictive covenants in credit facilities and debt instruments that limit dividends, additional debt, liens, asset sales, affiliate transactions, and impose financial ratio tests; risk of defaults and cross-defaults.
  - Dependence on distributions from subsidiaries and unconsolidated affiliates (e.g., CityCenter, MGM China, Operating Partnership) to meet obligations.
  - Uncertainty around refinancing timelines and availability/terms, potentially requiring asset sales or reduced capital spending.

- Master lease and leased property risks (MGP)
  - Significant fixed and percentage rent obligations with escalators under a triple-net master lease that reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to downturns.
  - Limitations on transferring lease obligations, continued rent requirements even if operations cease, and cross-collateralization of properties under a unitary lease.
  - Dependence on MGP as sole lessor for many properties; potential operational/financial issues at MGP could affect operations.
  - Governance complexities and potential conflicts of interest with overlapping directors/officers and special approval requirements for transactions over $25 million despite control via a Class B share.

- Business and competitive environment
  - Intense competition from destination resorts, regional casinos, online gaming, sports betting, and alternative lodging platforms; risk of new licenses and capacity in key markets (Las Vegas, Macau, domestic regions).
  - Concentration risk on the Las Vegas Strip, including reliance on air travel and a single major highway from Southern California.

- Regulatory and legal risks
  - Extensive gaming regulation across jurisdictions; suitability requirements for owners, partners, and key employees; potential for changing laws and interpretations (including DOJ’s Wire Act view).
  - Exposure to increased gaming taxes and other governmental fees; uncertainty around future tax regimes, including Macau exemptions.
  - Anti-money laundering and Bank Secrecy Act compliance obligations.
  - Other regulatory domains: alcohol, environmental, smoking restrictions (e.g., Macau smoking rooms), zoning/building codes, marketing/advertising.

- Macau- and China-specific risks
  - Subconcession termination, redemption, or non-extension risks; potential transfer of casino premises/equipment to Macau government without compensation; uncertainty around post-2020 regime (as of the reporting period).
  - Non-compete restrictions in Greater China outside MGM China.
  - Dependence on gaming promoters (VIP junkets), regulatory tightening of that segment, liquidity pressures, and credit exposure to promoters.
  - Macro factors: China economic conditions, anti-corruption measures, capital controls/ATM restrictions, facial recognition on ATMs, and limited labor importation; infrastructure constraints affecting visitation.

- Operational performance and strategy
  - Execution risk in the MGM 2020 cost-efficiency plan and variability in achieving targeted Adjusted EBITDA benefits.
  - Risks in paying regular dividends due to board discretion, debt covenants, holding company structure, and subsidiary performance.

- Development, construction, and asset management
  - Risks in future development/expansion projects: financing availability, permitting, design/engineering issues, labor/materials costs, contractor disputes, regulatory changes, delays, natural disasters, and penalties for missed regulatory deadlines.
  - Capital expenditure requirements for maintenance and refurbishments that may disrupt operations and displace revenue.
  - Co-investment risks (e.g., CityCenter), including shared control, partner financial instability, restrictive covenants, and potential funding obligations.

- Financial and accounting risks
  - Collectibility of gaming receivables/markers, especially from high-end customers and in foreign jurisdictions; potential tax on uncollectible winnings.
  - Potential impairments to goodwill, intangibles, and long-lived assets.
  - Tax risks, including changes in rates, timing, foreign withholding, and uncertainty around the recognition of foreign tax credit deferred tax assets and valuation allowances.

- External environment and ESG
  - Sensitivity to macroeconomics and consumer discretionary spend; shifts toward non-gaming preferences; exposure to U.S. and Far East economies.
  - Extreme weather/climate change impacts on properties and visitation; limitations and exclusions in property and business interruption insurance.
  - Energy price volatility affecting operating costs and customer travel.
  - Geopolitical events, terrorism, and war affecting air travel and insurance availability.

- Legal, labor, and compliance
  - Litigation and regulatory proceedings risk.
  - Significant unionized workforce; risks of strikes, negotiations, wage/benefit increases, and multi-employer pension plan liabilities.
  - International operations risks: legal/policy changes, staffing, tax, health outbreaks, political/economic instability, and currency fluctuations.
  - Anti-corruption compliance (FCPA and similar) risks, including potential severe penalties.

- Technology, data, and brand
  - Cybersecurity and data privacy risks (GDPR, CCPA); potential disruptions, reputational harm, regulatory penalties, and costs; reliance on third-party providers.
  - Trademark and intellectual property protection challenges, enforcement costs, and potential brand dilution.

- Corporate social responsibility and reputation
  - Reputational risks tied to ESG matters (diversity, environment, supply chain, human rights, philanthropy) that may affect customer and partner relationships and employee engagement.

- M&A and portfolio actions
  - Risks associated with acquisitions, alliances, and divestitures: integration, contingent liabilities, debt, systems compatibility, retention of key talent, and potential failure to realize anticipated benefits; uncertainty in executing asset sales.

- Other noted items
  - Potential increases in gaming taxes/fees could materially affect results.
  - Conflicts of interest may arise for directors/officers who also serve at MGM China.
  - Item 1B: Unresolved Staff Comments—none reported.

structure.summary:
- Operating Partnership and leasing: A subsidiary of the company leases the real estate assets of The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, and MGM National Harbor from a subsidiary of the Operating Partnership under a master lease. Aside from this, properties are not subject to major encumbrances. Reference is made to Note 9 for long-term debt details.
- Legal proceedings—October 1, 2017 Las Vegas shooting: Multiple lawsuits filed in Nevada and California allege negligence and seek damages for emotional distress, physical injury, medical expenses, economic damages, and wrongful death. Some actions were voluntarily dismissed with anticipated refilings; remaining cases were removed to federal court with motions to remand pending/anticipated. The company initiated declaratory relief actions in various federal districts. Mediation with plaintiffs’ counsel began in February 2019, and litigation is currently stayed pending mediation.
- Litigation outlook and insurance: Outcomes and costs are unpredictable; the company intends to defend the cases. It is reasonably possible some liability could be incurred, but no range of loss can currently be estimated under ASC 450-20. The company believes losses, if any, are unlikely to exceed available insurance. Insurers have not asserted coverage defenses affecting this evaluation, and the policies include a duty to defend that pays defense costs without eroding liability limits.
- Other legal matters: The company is involved in routine legal proceedings not expected to have a material adverse effect on financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.
- Mine safety: Not applicable.

structure.title: Selected Financial Data
structure.heading: Item 6. Selected Financial Data
structure.start_phrase:
The following reflects se
lected historical financial data that should be read in conjunction with “Item 7 – Management’s Discussion and Analysis of FinancialCondition
 and Results of Operations” and the consolidated financial statements and notes thereto included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Excerpt from an Annual Report on Form 10-K covering Item 6 (Selected Financial Data for 2014–2018) and the Item 7 MD&A Executive Overview.

- Selected Financial Data (2014–2018):
  - Net revenues grew to $11.8B in 2018 from $10.8B in 2017 and $9.5B in 2016 (versus $10.1B in 2014).
  - Operating income declined to $1.47B in 2018 from $1.71B in 2017 and $2.08B in 2016; 2015 showed an operating loss.
  - Net income was $584M in 2018 versus $2.09B in 2017 and $1.24B in 2016; losses in 2015.
  - Net income attributable to MGM Resorts International was $467M in 2018 versus $1.95B in 2017 and $1.10B in 2016.
  - EPS: Basic $0.82 and Diluted $0.81 in 2018 (versus $3.38/$3.34 in 2017 and $1.94/$1.92 in 2016). Dividends initiated in 2017 and increased to $0.48 per share in 2018.
  - Year-end balance sheet: Total assets $30.2B, total debt $15.2B, stockholders’ equity $10.5B in 2018. Shares outstanding decreased to 527.5M.

- Events affecting year-to-year comparability:
  - Acquisitions/Dispositions/Significant transactions:
    - 2015: $23M gain on sale of Circus Circus Reno and 50% of Silver Legacy.
    - 2016: $401M share of CityCenter gain on sale of The Shops at Crystals; $1.1B net proceeds from MGP IPO; $430M gain on acquiring Boyd’s Borgata stake; consolidation of Borgata; opening of MGM National Harbor.
    - 2018: Openings of MGM Cotai and MGM Springfield; MGP acquired Northfield; $45M gain on sale of 50% interest in Grand Victoria.
  - Other notable items:
    - 2014: $29M impairment on Grand Victoria investment.
    - 2015: $1.5B goodwill impairment at MGM China; $17M Grand Victoria impairment; $80M share of CityCenter construction-litigation settlement gain.
    - 2016: $67M loss on early debt retirement; $152M expense exiting NV Energy’s bundled sales system (followed by a $45M 2017 gain on exit fee modification).
    - 2017: $44M loss on early debt retirement; $36M Borgata property tax settlement gain; $1.4B tax benefit from the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
    - 2018: $20M tax expense related to the Tax Act; $24M business interruption insurance proceeds from the Oct. 1, 2017 Las Vegas incident.
  - Accounting change: Adoption of ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) on a full retrospective basis affecting 2015–2018 data.

- MD&A Executive Overview highlights:
  - Business model: Ownership/operation of casino resorts with gaming and non-gaming amenities; heavy reliance on operating cash flow to fund capex, development, and debt service; focus on capital allocation and shareholder returns alongside strategic growth.
  - Market conditions and operating drivers:
    - Las Vegas: 2018 visitor volume down 0.2%, Strip REVPAR up 1%, Strip gaming revenue up 2%; Park MGM repositioning/rebranding caused disruption to results.
    - Regional Operations: Competitive pressures; Borgata impacted by two new Atlantic City openings in June 2018; MGM Springfield opening in August 2018 benefited results.
    - Macau: 2018 market GGR up 14%; visitor arrivals up 10% and overnight visitors up 7%; long-term growth expected from mainland China penetration and infrastructure; MGM Cotai opening in Feb 2018 contributed to growth.
  - Corporate/structural items:
    - Master lease with MGP under which major resort real estate assets are leased to the operating tenant; MGP and its Operating Partnership are consolidated, and intercompany transactions (including lease) are eliminated.
    - July 2018: MGP acquired Northfield; Hard Rock affiliate engaged to manage the property.
  - Strategic initiatives:
    - January 2019 launch of MGM 2020, a company-wide optimization and digital transformation program targeting $300M annualized Adjusted EBITDA benefit by 2021 ($200M by end of 2020, plus $100M by end of 2021).

structure.title: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: Our primary business is the ownership and operation of casino resorts, which offer gaming, hotel, convention, dining, entertainment, retail and other resortamenities.
structure.summary:
- Document type and scope: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for MGM Resorts International covering 2018 results with comparisons to 2017 and 2016, plus liquidity, capital resources, critical accounting policies, and market risk.
- Business overview: Cash-based revenue model from casino resorts (gaming and non-gaming amenities); ongoing reinvestment; focus on capital allocation, access/cost of capital, and strategic initiatives.
- Market context:
  - Las Vegas: 2018 visitor volume down 0.2%, Strip REVPAR up 1%, gaming revenue up 2%; Park MGM rebranding caused disruption.
  - Regional: Intensifying competition; negative impact from two new Atlantic City openings; benefit from MGM Springfield opening.
  - Macau: 2018 GGR up 14%; arrivals up 10% and overnight up 7%; long-term growth outlook; MGM Cotai opened February 2018 and contributed meaningfully.
- Key transactions and structure:
  - Master lease with MGM Growth Properties (MGP) covering major properties; intercompany transactions eliminated in consolidation.
  - MGP acquired Northfield (Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park) in July 2018; Hard Rock affiliate continues to manage.
  - MGM 2020 initiative announced January 2019 targeting $300 million annualized Adjusted EBITDA uplift (by end of 2021) via cost reductions, centralization, and digital/technology investments.
- Key performance indicators:
  - Gaming: table drop/slots handle and normal hold ranges for Las Vegas and Regional; MGM China VIP turnover and typical win percentages.
  - Hotel: occupancy, ADR, REVPAR (with note on complimentary room pricing).
- Consolidated results:
  - Net revenues rose 9% in 2018 to $11.76 billion (driven by MGM Cotai and MGM Springfield).
  - Operating income fell 14% (ramp-up costs and depreciation at new properties, Park MGM disruption, higher corporate expense); included gain on Grand Victoria sale and business interruption proceeds; prior periods had notable one-time items.
  - Net income impacted by 2017’s large non-cash tax benefit from U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA).
- Segment performance and metrics:
  - Las Vegas Strip Resorts: Casino revenue down 2% (higher incentives); rooms revenue flat with 91% occupancy, ADR $161, REVPAR $147; F&B down 1% (rebranding closures), entertainment/other up 1% (parking, minibars); table drop and slots handle stable with slight hold improvement.
  - Regional Operations: Casino revenue up 10% (MGM Springfield, strong National Harbor); rooms/F&B/other mixed with growth from Springfield and headliner shows; continued competitive pressures; gaming volumes and win rates improved.
  - MGM China: Net revenue up 32% (Cotai contribution); main floor win +33%, VIP win +12% after Cotai VIP junket rooms opened; 2018 VIP win 3.0%, main floor win 18.4%.
  - Corporate and other: Includes management services, reimbursed costs, and MGP’s Northfield revenue starting July 2018.
- Adjusted EBITDA (non-GAAP):
  - Total 2018: $2.81 billion (slightly below 2017).
  - Las Vegas Strip Resorts: Down 4%; margin 29.8% (down 115 bps) due to casino revenue declines and Park MGM disruption (partially offset by insurance).
  - Regional Operations: Up 4%; margin 25.9% (down 114 bps) due to Springfield ramp and lower Borgata margin amid competition/weather.
  - MGM China: Up 6% (7% ex-intercompany license fees); margin 23.2% (down from 28.8%) reflecting Cotai ramp and lower win at MGM Macau.
  - Corporate/other: Lower due to higher stock-based comp and corporate costs; includes Northfield EBITDA.
- Specific charges and items:
  - Preopening and start-up expenses rose to $151 million (Springfield, Park MGM; offset by lower Cotai after opening).
  - Property transactions included gain on sale of Grand Victoria; other routine asset transactions.
  - Income from unconsolidated affiliates: CityCenter contributions; 2018 included gain tied to Mandarin Oriental sale; 2016 included large Crystals sale gain.
- Non-operating results and taxes:
  - Interest expense up on higher average debt and rates; capitalized interest down post Cotai opening and Springfield completion.
  - Other expenses improved vs. 2017 due to prior-year debt extinguishment losses.
  - Taxes: 2018 rate benefited from lower U.S. rate and Macau dividend tax reversal (offset by TCJA SAB 118 effects); 2017 included a large non-recurring tax benefit from TCJA deferred tax remeasurement.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Cash flows: 2018 operating cash flow $1.72 billion (down vs. 2017 on working capital timing at MGM China, lower operating income, higher interest); investing uses increased (Northfield acquisition offset by lower capex and Grand Victoria proceeds); financing provided cash (net borrowings).
  - Capital expenditures: 2018 $1.5 billion (Cotai closeout, Springfield, Park MGM rebranding, convention expansion, room/venue remodels); prior years heavier due to Cotai and National Harbor builds.
  - Debt activity: 2018 net borrowings ~$2.2 billion (new 5.750% 2025 notes; draws on MGM Resorts, MGM China, and Operating Partnership facilities); detail of 2016–2017 issuances/repayments provided.
  - Capital returns: Stock repurchases ($1.3 billion in 2018 under new $2.0 billion authorization; $328 million in 2017) and dividends ($0.12/share quarterly in 2018; $0.11 in 2017).
  - MGP Operating Partnership distributions and MGP dividends; MGM China dividends to shareholders.
  - Year-end 2018 liquidity/debt: $1.5 billion cash; $15.3 billion total debt; outlines expected 2019 capex and funding plan.
  - 2019 events: Closed Empire City acquisition (mix of cash, stock, assumed debt); Operating Partnership issued 5.75% 2027 notes; redemption of 8.625% 2019 notes.
- Off-balance-sheet arrangements: Primarily investments in unconsolidated affiliates (notably CityCenter); interest rate hedges at Operating Partnership.
- Contractual obligations: Schedule of debt maturities, expected interest payments, operating leases, and other commitments.
- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Allowance for doubtful casino accounts (including marker play and foreign collections; detailed reserve levels and sensitivities).
  - Capitalization and depreciation policies for fixed assets, including interest capitalization.
  - Impairment testing for long-lived assets, goodwill, and indefinite-lived intangibles (methodologies, judgments, recent results).
  - Investments in unconsolidated affiliates impairment considerations.
  - Income taxes, valuation allowances, uncertain tax positions, and audit status.
- Market risk disclosures:
  - Interest rate risk: Mix of fixed/variable debt; interest rate swaps in place and additional swaps effective end of 2019; sensitivity by maturity buckets.
  - Foreign currency risk: Exposure via MGM China (HKD functional currency); potential peg changes; illustrative sensitivity of cash and debt to FX moves.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
In
 addition to the inherent risks associated with our normal operations, we are also exposed to additional market risks.
structure.summary:
- Section Item 7A outlines quantitative and qualitative disclosures about market risk.
- Primary market risk is interest rate risk from variable-rate long-term debt; the company manages exposure via a mix of fixed- and variable-rate borrowings and uses interest rate swaps on the Operating Partnership’s term loan B. No trading or speculative derivatives are used.
- Interest rate sensitivity: fixed-rate debt doesn’t affect earnings/cash flow until maturity/refinancing; variable-rate exposure can impact future earnings and cash flows.
- As of December 31, 2018, variable-rate borrowings were about 31% of total after giving effect to existing interest rate swaps ($500 million at 1.764% and $700 million at 1.901%). Additional swaps entered in December 2018 will be effective December 31, 2019 for $400 million at 2.735%, resulting in a combined weighted average pay rate of 2.066%.
- Debt profile (2018): Fixed-rate debt totaled $9.251 billion (fair value $9.179 billion) with an overall average rate of 6.3%; Variable-rate debt totaled $6.002 billion (fair value $5.893 billion) with an overall average rate of 4.6%. Maturities are spread across 2019–Thereafter with disclosed average rates by bucket.
- Foreign currency risk primarily relates to MGM China operations (MGM Macau and MGM Cotai), with exposure tied to the Hong Kong dollar’s peg to the U.S. dollar; policy/economic changes could affect exchange rates.
- FX sensitivity as of December 31, 2018: a 1% increase in HKD/USD would raise the carrying value of cash by $5 million; a 1% decrease would lower the carrying value of debt by $25 million.

structure.title: Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.heading: Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.summary:
- Scope: Consolidated financial statements for MGM Resorts International and subsidiaries for years ended December 31, 2018, 2017, and 2016, plus notes on organization and recent transactions.

- Consolidated Balance Sheets (2018 vs 2017):
  - Total assets: $30.21B vs $29.16B.
  - Cash and cash equivalents: $1.53B vs $1.50B.
  - Property and equipment, net: $20.73B vs $19.64B.
  - Other assets include goodwill ($1.82B) and intangible assets, net ($3.94B).
  - Total current liabilities: $2.95B vs $3.14B.
  - Long-term debt, net: $15.09B vs $12.75B; deferred income taxes, net: $1.34B vs $1.30B.
  - Total stockholders’ equity: $10.47B vs $11.61B; MGM Resorts International stockholders’ equity: $6.51B vs $7.58B; noncontrolling interests: $3.96B vs $4.03B.
  - Shares outstanding decreased to 527.5M from 566.3M.

- Consolidated Statements of Operations:
  - Revenues grew to $11.76B in 2018 (2017: $10.80B; 2016: $9.48B), led by:
    - Casino: $5.75B (2017: $5.02B; 2016: $4.11B).
    - Rooms: $2.21B; Food & beverage: $1.96B; Entertainment/retail/other: $1.41B; Reimbursed costs: $0.43B.
  - Expenses increased across operating categories; depreciation and amortization: $1.18B (2017: $0.99B).
  - Operating income: $1.47B (2017: $1.71B; 2016: $2.08B).
  - Non-operating net expense: $(0.84)B (higher interest and other items).
  - Income before income taxes: $0.63B; income tax provision (benefit): $(0.05)B in 2018 vs a large tax benefit of $1.13B in 2017.
  - Net income: $584M (2017: $2.09B; 2016: $1.24B); attributable to MGMRI: $467M (2017: $1.95B; 2016: $1.10B).
  - EPS: basic $0.82, diluted $0.81 (2017: $3.38/$3.34; 2016: $1.94/$1.92).
  - Notable items: NV Energy exit credit in 2017, expense in 2016; 2016 gain on Borgata transaction.

- Comprehensive Income:
  - Includes foreign currency translation losses and gains on cash flow hedges; accumulated other comprehensive loss increased (more negative) in 2018.

- Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows:
  - Operating cash flow: $1.72B (2017: $2.21B; 2016: $1.53B).
  - Investing cash flow: $(2.08)B used, driven by capex $(1.49)B and Northfield acquisition $(1.03)B; offset by distributions from unconsolidated affiliates.
  - Financing cash flow: $0.39B provided; key activities include $1.0B new long-term debt, $1.24B net short-term borrowings, $(1.28)B share repurchases, $(0.26)B common dividends, and NCI distributions.
  - Ending cash: $1.53B.

- Consolidated Statements of Stockholders’ Equity (2016–2018):
  - Movements reflect net income, OCI changes, stock-based compensation, common dividends ($0.44/share in 2017; $0.48/share in 2018), share repurchases ($327.5M in 2017; $1.283B in 2018), MGP-related transactions, and distributions to noncontrolling interests.

- Notes—Organization and Structure:
  - Company overview: Holding company owning/operating integrated casino, hotel, and entertainment resorts in Las Vegas (e.g., Bellagio, MGM Grand, The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, Circus Circus) and U.S. regional markets (MGM Grand Detroit, MGM National Harbor, MGM Springfield opened Aug 24, 2018; Borgata; Beau Rivage; Gold Strike). Additional assets include The Park and several golf courses.
  - MGM Growth Properties (MGP): Consolidated UPREIT with Operating Partnership; two share classes (Class A and a single Class B held by the Company). The Company controls voting through Class B and held 73.3% of Operating Partnership units at Dec 31, 2018; units are exchangeable into MGP Class A shares or cash.
  - Master lease: Company (tenant) leases real estate of multiple properties (e.g., The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM, Excalibur, The Park, Gold Strike Tunica, MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Borgata, MGM National Harbor) from MGP’s Operating Partnership (landlord).
  - Recent transactions:
    - July 2018: MGP acquired Northfield Park Associates (Hard Rock Rocksino Northfield Park); Hard Rock continues as manager.
    - September 2018: Company agreed to acquire Northfield’s operating assets from MGP; to be added to the master lease (expected close 1H 2019).
    - January 2019: Company acquired Empire City Casino operations and real property; MGP then acquired the developed real property and leased it back to the Company via the master lease amendment.

  - Las Vegas resorts: Bellagio, MGM Grand Las Vegas (including management of The Signature), The Mirage, Mandalay Bay, Luxor, New York-New York, Park MGM (rebranded from Monte Carlo in May 2018), Excalibur, Circus Circus.

nodes.title: BASIS OF PRESENTATION AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.heading: NOTE 2 — BASIS OF PRESENTATION AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.start_phrase: For entities not determined to be a variable interest entity (“VIE”), the Company consolidates such entities in which the Company owns 100% of the equity.
nodes.summary:
- Ownership and operations:
  - Holds ~56% controlling interest in MGM China (MGM Grand Paradise), which owns and operates MGM Macau and MGM Cotai (opened February 13, 2018), along with related gaming subconcession and land concessions in Macau.
  - Owns 50% and manages CityCenter (with Infinity World/Dubai World owning the other 50%), comprising Aria and Vdara; CityCenter sold the Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas and adjacent retail parcels on August 30, 2018.
  - Co-owns the Las Vegas Arena Company (T-Mobile Arena) with AEG (each 42.5%) and Athena Arena, LLC (15%); manages T-Mobile Arena and leases MGM Grand Garden Arena to the Las Vegas Arena Company.
  - In August 2018, sold its 50% interest in the Grand Victoria riverboat casino in Elgin, Illinois.

- Segment reporting:
  - As of Q4 2018, reorganized into three reportable segments: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China, reflecting expansion of regional operations.

- Basis of presentation and consolidation policies:
  - Consolidates entities it controls (including those with less than 100% ownership) and records noncontrolling interests accordingly; uses the equity method for 50% or less owned affiliates where it has significant influence or joint control.
  - Eliminates all intercompany balances and transactions in consolidation.
  - Evaluates and consolidates variable interest entities (VIEs) when the Company is the primary beneficiary (has power over key activities and exposure to significant benefits/losses); reassesses upon changes in arrangements or ownership.

- MGP (MGM Growth Properties) as a VIE:
  - Determined to be a VIE because Class A equity holders lack sufficient power; the Company consolidates MGP due to majority voting power via the single Class B share and rights to significant benefits through exchangeable Operating Partnership units.
  - Records MGP’s 26.7% ownership interest in the Operating Partnership as noncontrolling interest.
  - As of December 31, 2018, on a consolidated basis, MGP had approximately $11.0 billion in total assets (primarily real estate) and $5.1 billion in total liabilities (primarily indebtedness).

nodes.title: Principles of consolidation.
nodes.heading: 2.1 Principles of consolidation.
nodes.start_phrase: For entities not determined to be a variable interest entity (“VIE”), the Company consolidates such entities in which the Company owns 100% of the equity.
nodes.summary:
- The Company holds a ~56% controlling interest in MGM China, which owns MGM Grand Paradise, operating MGM Macau and MGM Cotai (opened February 13, 2018), along with related gaming subconcession and land concessions in Macau.
- The Company owns 50% and manages CityCenter Holdings, LLC; the other 50% is owned by Dubai World’s subsidiary. CityCenter includes Aria and Vdara. On August 30, 2018, CityCenter sold the Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas and adjacent retail parcels.
- The Company and AEG each own 42.5% of Las Vegas Arena Company, which owns T-Mobile Arena; Athena Arena owns the remaining 15%. The Company manages T-Mobile Arena and leases MGM Grand Garden Arena to the Las Vegas Arena Company.
- In August 2018, the Company and its joint venture partner sold their 50% interest in the Grand Victoria riverboat casino in Elgin, Illinois.
- In Q4 2018, the Company reorganized into three reportable segments: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China, reflecting expansion of regional operations.
- Basis of presentation and consolidation policies: the Company consolidates entities it controls (including certain less-than-100% owned entities), applies the equity method to unconsolidated affiliates where it has significant influence or joint control, and eliminates intercompany balances.
- Variable interest entity (VIE) framework: the Company identifies and consolidates VIEs where it is the primary beneficiary (has power over significant activities and exposure to significant benefits or losses), reassessing upon changes in facts or arrangements.
- MGP is deemed a VIE; the Company is the primary beneficiary due to majority voting power via a Class B share and rights from exchangeable Operating Partnership units, so it consolidates MGP. MGP’s 26.7% Operating Partnership interest is recorded as noncontrolling interest. As of December 31, 2018, MGP had $11.0 billion in total assets (primarily real estate) and $5.1 billion in total liabilities (primarily indebtedness).

nodes.title: Management’s use of estimates.
nodes.heading: 2.2 Management’s use of estimates.
nodes.start_phrase: The consolidated financial statements have been prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation and estimates: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP; management uses estimates and assumptions affecting asset/liability amounts, contingent items, and revenues/expenses; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Fair value defined as exit price in an orderly transaction, using a hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs). Used for long-lived assets, unconsolidated investments, cost method investments, business combinations, goodwill/intangibles, and certain financial instruments. Level 1/2 inputs used for long-term debt fair value disclosures (Note 9). Level 2/3 inputs used for assets acquired and liabilities assumed in the Northfield and Borgata transactions (Note 4).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Investments and interest-bearing instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market. Book overdrafts recorded as accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit issued to approved customers and gaming promoters after credit checks. As of Dec 31, 2018 and 2017, about 62% and 40% of gross casino receivables were from foreign customers (primarily Asia), exposing the Company to country/region-specific risks. Receivables are non-interest bearing; write-offs when deemed uncollectible; recoveries recognized when received. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific account reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; management believes no unreserved significant concentrations of credit risk existed at Dec 31, 2018.
- Inventories: Primarily food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies; carried at lower of cost or net realizable value. Average cost for food/beverage and supplies; cost method for retail merchandise.
- Property and equipment: Stated at cost; significant amounts recognized at fair value at acquisition dates due to business combinations. Gains/losses on disposals recognized in earnings; maintenance expensed as incurred. Accrued property and equipment within accounts payable of $47 million (2018) and $28 million (2017); construction retention in other long-term liabilities of $2 million (2018) and $34 million (2017).
- Depreciation: Straight-line over estimated useful lives—buildings and improvements (15–40 years), land improvements (10–20 years), furniture and fixtures (3–20 years), equipment (3–15 years).
- Long-lived asset impairment: Classification as held for sale requires an authorized commitment to sell at a reasonable price and active marketing. Held-for-sale assets recorded at the lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell, estimated via comparable sales, offers, or discounted cash flows. Assets held and used are evaluated for impairment (discussion continues beyond excerpt).

nodes.title: Fair value measurements.
nodes.heading: 2.3 Fair value measurements.
nodes.start_phrase: Fair value measurements affect the Company’s accounting and impairment assessments of its long-lived assets, investments in unconsolidated affiliates, cost method investments, assets acquired and liabilities assumed in an acquisition, and goodwill and other intangible assets.
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation and use of estimates: Financial statements prepared under US GAAP; management makes estimates and assumptions affecting reported assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and contingencies; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Definition of fair value and hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs for similar assets, Level 3 unobservable inputs). Fair value impacts accounting for long‑lived assets, investments in unconsolidated affiliates, cost method investments, acquisition accounting, goodwill and intangibles, and certain financial instruments. Company used Level 1 and 2 for long‑term debt fair value disclosures (Note 9) and Level 2 and 3 in measuring assets and liabilities in the Northfield and Borgata acquisitions (Note 4).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Include investments and interest‑bearing instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market; book overdrafts from cash management recorded as accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit issued after background checks; significant concentration of receivables from foreign (primarily Asian) customers (about 62% at Dec 31, 2018; 40% at Dec 31, 2017), with related collectability risk. Receivables are non‑interest bearing, recorded at cost, written off when uncollectible, with recoveries recognized when received. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; management believes no unreserved significant concentrations at Dec 31, 2018.
- Inventories: Primarily food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies; stated at lower of cost or net realizable value. Cost determined by average cost for F&B and supplies; retail merchandise by cost method.
- Property and equipment: Carried at cost; significant assets recognized at fair value when acquired in business combinations. Gains/losses on disposals recognized in income; maintenance expensed as incurred. Accruals at Dec 31, 2018/2017 include $47m/$28m in accounts payable and $2m/$34m in construction retention within other long‑term liabilities.
- Depreciation: Straight‑line over estimated useful lives—buildings/improvements 15–40 years; land improvements 10–20; furniture/fixtures 3–20; equipment 3–15.
- Long‑lived asset impairment: Evaluation based on classification as held for sale or held and used. Held‑for‑sale classification requires management commitment to a plan at a reasonable price and active marketing; measurement at lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell based on comparable sales, offers, or discounted cash flows.

nodes.title: Cash and cash equivalents.
nodes.heading: 2.4 Cash and cash equivalents.
nodes.start_phrase: Cash and cash equivalents include investments and interest bearing instruments with maturities of 90 days or less at the date of acquisition.
nodes.summary:
- Management’s use of estimates: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP require estimates and assumptions affecting reported assets, liabilities, contingencies, revenues, and expenses; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Applied to long-lived assets, investments (including unconsolidated affiliates and cost method), acquisition accounting (assets/liabilities assumed), goodwill and intangibles, and certain financial instruments; fair value defined as exit price with Level 1, 2, and 3 input hierarchy. Company used Level 1–2 for long-term debt disclosures and Level 2–3 for Northfield and Borgata acquisition accounting.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Investments with maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market; book overdrafts recorded in accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit granted after credit checks; significant foreign exposure (62% in 2018; 40% in 2017, primarily Asia), with potential collectability risk from foreign economic conditions; non-interest-bearing receivables recorded at cost; write-offs upon deemed uncollectible; recoveries recognized when received; allowance based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; no unreserved significant concentrations as of Dec 31, 2018.
- Inventories: Primarily food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies; stated at lower of cost or net realizable value; average cost for F&B and supplies; cost method for retail merchandise.
- Property and equipment: Stated at cost (many assets initially recognized at fair value via business combinations); gains/losses on disposals in earnings; maintenance expensed; accrued amounts for capex and construction retention disclosed. Depreciated straight-line over estimated useful lives: buildings/improvements 15–40 years; land improvements 10–20; furniture/fixtures 3–20; equipment 3–15.
- Long-lived asset impairment: Evaluation depends on classification as held for sale or held and used; held-for-sale criteria include authorized plan to sell at a reasonable price and active marketing; measured at lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell based on comps, offers, or DCF.

nodes.title: Accounts receivable and credit risk.
nodes.heading: 2.5 Accounts receivable and credit risk.
nodes.start_phrase: Financial instruments that potentially subject the Company to concentrations of credit risk consist primarily of casino accounts receivable.
nodes.summary:
- Explains management’s use of estimates under U.S. GAAP and how assumptions affect reported assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and contingencies; notes actual results may differ.
- Details fair value measurements: definition (exit price), the Level 1–3 input hierarchy, and areas impacted (long‑lived assets, investments in unconsolidated affiliates, cost‑method investments, acquisition accounting, goodwill and intangibles, and certain financial instruments). Specifies use of Level 1/2 inputs for long‑term debt disclosures and Level 2/3 inputs for the Northfield and Borgata acquisition accounting.
- Defines cash and cash equivalents (maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market) and treatment of book overdrafts (recorded as accounts payable or construction payable).
- Describes accounts receivable and credit risk: concentration in casino receivables; credit issuance to vetted customers and gaming promoters; significant foreign exposure (62% in 2018; 40% in 2017, primarily Asia); non‑interest‑bearing recognition at cost; write‑off and recovery practices; allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; management’s view that no unreserved significant concentrations existed at 12/31/2018.
- Outlines inventory accounting: primarily food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies; carried at lower of cost or net realizable value; average cost for F&B and supplies; cost method for retail merchandise.
- Summarizes property and equipment policies: recorded at cost (fair value at acquisition for business combinations); gains/losses on disposals recognized in income; maintenance expensed; accrued amounts related to property and equipment and construction retention disclosed (2018/2017); straight‑line depreciation with estimated useful lives (buildings 15–40 years; land improvements 10–20; furniture and fixtures 3–20; equipment 3–15).
- Addresses long‑lived asset impairment: classification criteria for held‑for‑sale assets (commitment to sell, reasonable price relative to fair value, active marketing) and measurement at the lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell using comparable sales, offers, or discounted cash flow; indicates the discussion for assets held and used continues beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: Inventories.
nodes.heading: 2.6 Inventories.
nodes.start_phrase: Inventories consist primarily of food and beverage, retail merchandise and operating supplies, and are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value.
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation and use of estimates: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP; management makes estimates and assumptions affecting assets, liabilities, contingent items, revenues, and expenses; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Definition of fair value and three-level input hierarchy (Level 1, 2, 3). Fair value informs accounting and impairment for long-lived assets, investments (including unconsolidated and cost-method), acquisition accounting (assets/liabilities assumed), goodwill and intangibles, and certain financial instruments. Company uses Level 1/2 for long-term debt disclosures and Level 2/3 in acquisition accounting (e.g., Northfield and Borgata).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Includes cash, investments, and interest-bearing instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market value. Book overdrafts recorded as accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Casino credit issued after creditworthiness checks. Significant foreign exposure—approximately 62% (2018) and 40% (2017) of gross casino receivables from foreign customers, primarily Asia—subject to economic/event risk. Receivables are non-interest bearing, recorded at cost; write-offs when deemed uncollectible with recoveries recognized upon receipt. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions; no unprovided significant concentrations as of Dec 31, 2018.
