- Property and equipment (P&E): Stated at cost; significant amounts initially recognized at fair value due to acquisition accounting. Gains/losses on disposals recognized in income; maintenance expensed. Accrued P&E balances disclosed in accounts payable and construction retention. Depreciation straight-line over estimated useful lives: buildings/improvements 15–40 years; land improvements 10–20 years; furniture/fixtures 3–20 years; equipment 3–15 years.
- Long-lived asset impairment: Evaluation based on held-for-sale versus held-and-used classification. Held-for-sale criteria include approved plan, reasonable pricing versus fair value, and active marketing; measured at lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell using comparable sales, offers, or discounted cash flows. (Discussion of held-and-used impairment begins but is truncated.)

nodes.title: Property and equipment.
nodes.heading: 2.7 Property and equipment.
nodes.start_phrase: Property and equipment are stated at cost.
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation and use of estimates: Financial statements prepared under U.S. GAAP; management makes estimates and assumptions affecting reported assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses, and contingencies; actual results may differ.
- Fair value measurements: Defines fair value and the Level 1–3 input hierarchy; impacts accounting and impairment for long‑lived assets, financial instruments, acquisitions, goodwill, and intangibles. Uses Level 1 and 2 for long‑term debt disclosures (Note 9) and Levels 2 and 3 for Northfield and Borgata acquisition accounting (Note 4).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Investments with original maturities of 90 days or less, carried at cost approximating market; book overdrafts presented in accounts payable or construction payable.
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Primarily casino receivables extended to vetted customers/promoters; significant foreign exposure (approx. 62% in 2018; 40% in 2017, primarily Asia). Non‑interest bearing, with write‑off and recovery policies; allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific reviews, history, and current conditions; no unreserved significant concentrations at 12/31/18.
- Inventories: Food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies at lower of cost or net realizable value; average cost for F&B and supplies; cost method for retail merchandise.
- Property and equipment: Stated at cost (many assets initially recognized at fair value via business combinations). Maintenance expensed; disclosures of accrued property/equipment and construction retention. Depreciated straight‑line over: buildings/improvements 15–40 yrs; land improvements 10–20 yrs; furniture/fixtures 3–20 yrs; equipment 3–15 yrs.
- Long‑lived asset impairment: Classification as held for sale vs. held and used. Held for sale measured at lower of carrying amount or fair value less costs to sell. Held and used tested when indicators exist via undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, impairment measured via discounted cash flows. Development assets include remaining construction costs; impairments recorded in operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Interest on major development/construction capitalized; if no project‑specific debt, uses weighted‑average borrowing cost; capitalization ceases when substantially complete or if activity is suspended beyond a brief period.
- Investments in and advances to unconsolidated affiliates: Equity method accounting with adjustments for share of earnings/losses and basis differences; excess distributions treated as return of investment (investing cash inflows). Classifies related results as operating or non‑operating based on alignment with core operations. Impairment evaluated for other‑than‑temporary declines using DCF and market multiples (Note 6).
- Goodwill and other intangible assets: Annual impairment tests in Q4 and upon triggering events; no impairments in 2016–2018. Option for qualitative “step zero” assessment considering macro/industry factors, performance, entity‑specific events, and prior test headroom. Quantitative tests use DCF with market discount/cap rates and market multiples; adopted 2017 simplification eliminating Step 2. Indefinite‑lived intangibles tested via DCF (license rights) and relief‑from‑royalty (trademarks); recognize loss if fair value < carrying amount.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue from contracts with customers includes casino wagers, hotel rooms, food and beverage, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.

nodes.title: Capitalized interest.
nodes.heading: 2.8 Capitalized interest.
nodes.start_phrase: The interest cost associated with major development and construction projects is capitalized and included in the cost of the project.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of long‑lived assets: Reviewed when indicators arise by comparing undiscounted future cash flows to carrying value. If undiscounted cash flows don’t exceed carrying value, record an impairment based on fair value (typically via discounted cash flow). For assets under development, projected cash flows include remaining construction costs. All impairment losses are recorded as operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Interest on major development/construction projects is capitalized into project cost. When no project-specific debt exists, use the weighted-average borrowing rate. Capitalization ends when the project is substantially complete or when development is suspended beyond a brief period.
- Investments in and advances to unconsolidated affiliates: Accounted for under the equity method, adjusting carrying value for the Company’s share of earnings/losses, basis difference amortization, contributions, and distributions. Distributions exceeding equity earnings are treated as returns of investment and shown as investing cash inflows. Operating results, gains, and impairments from these affiliates are included in operating income (as extensions of core operations), while non-operating items are in non-operating income/loss. Impairment is evaluated upon indicators of “other‑than‑temporary” decline using fair value estimates based on discounted cash flows and market multiples, considering intent and ability to hold.
- Goodwill and other intangible assets: Goodwill represents excess purchase price over fair value of net assets acquired. Goodwill and indefinite‑lived intangibles are tested at least annually (in Q4) and interperiod when warranted; no impairments were recorded for 2018, 2017, or 2016. A qualitative “step zero” assessment may be performed considering macro, industry, performance, and entity-specific factors; if likely impaired, proceed to quantitative testing. Quantitative tests use discounted cash flows with market discount/terminal rates and peer multiples. From January 1, 2017, the simplified guidance eliminates Step 2; impairment equals the excess of carrying value over fair value, capped at recorded goodwill. Indefinite‑lived intangibles: license rights tested via DCF; trademarks via relief-from-royalty; impairments recognized if fair value is below carrying amount.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue from contracts with customers includes casino wagers, hotel rooms, food and beverage, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.

nodes.title: Investments in and advances to unconsolidated affiliates.
nodes.heading: 2.9 Investments in and advances to unconsolidated affiliates.
nodes.start_phrase: The Company has investments in unconsolidated affiliates accounted for under the equity method.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of long‑lived assets: Assess recoverability when indicators exist using undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, measure impairment at fair value via discounted cash flows. Include remaining construction costs for in‑development assets. Record all impairment losses as operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Capitalize interest on major development/construction projects using specific borrowing rates or the weighted‑average cost of outstanding borrowings; cease capitalization when substantially complete or when activity is suspended beyond a brief period.
- Investments in unconsolidated affiliates: Accounted for under the equity method with adjustments for share of earnings/losses and basis difference amortization; classify related results as operating or non‑operating consistent with core operations. Distributions in excess of equity income are returns of investment and presented as investing cash inflows. Evaluate for other‑than‑temporary impairment using DCF and market multiples, considering intent and ability to hold.
- Goodwill and other intangible assets: Test at least annually (in Q4) and upon triggering events. Option to perform qualitative “step zero” assessment; if needed, perform quantitative tests using DCF and market approaches. Adopted 2017 guidance eliminating former Step 2 for goodwill—impairment equals excess of carrying amount over fair value (capped at goodwill). License rights tested via DCF; trademarks via relief‑from‑royalty. No impairments recorded in 2016–2018.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue streams include casino wagers, hotel rooms, food and beverage, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.

nodes.title: Goodwill and other intangible assets.
nodes.heading: 2.10 Goodwill and other intangible assets.
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill represents the excess of purchase price over fair market value of net assets acquired in business combinations.
nodes.summary:
- Long-lived assets impairment: The company reviews assets held for use and held for sale when indicators arise, tests recoverability using undiscounted cash flows, and records impairments based on fair value (typically discounted cash flows). For assets under development, projected cash flows include remaining construction costs. Recognized impairments are recorded as operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Interest on major development and construction projects is capitalized at the weighted-average borrowing rate when no project-specific debt exists. Capitalization stops when the project is substantially complete or when development is suspended for more than a brief period.
- Investments in unconsolidated affiliates: Accounted for under the equity method with carrying value adjusted for the company’s share of earnings/losses, basis difference amortization, and capital contributions/distributions. Distributions exceeding equity earnings are treated as returns of investment and shown as investing cash inflows. Operating vs. non-operating results related to these investments are classified consistent with their role as extensions of core operations. Impairment is evaluated for other-than-temporary declines using fair value estimates from discounted cash flows and market multiples.
- Goodwill and other intangible assets: Goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are tested at least annually (fourth quarter) and upon triggering events; no impairments were recorded in 2016–2018. A qualitative “step zero” assessment may be performed considering macro, industry, performance, entity-specific factors, changes in net asset composition, prior excess fair value over carrying value, and time since the last quantitative test. If needed, a quantitative test uses discounted cash flows with market discount rates and terminal capitalization rates plus market multiples. From January 1, 2017, impairment is measured as the excess of carrying value over fair value (elimination of former Step 2). License rights are tested via discounted cash flows; trademarks via the relief-from-royalty method.
- Revenue recognition: Revenue arises from casino wagers, hotel rooms, food and beverage, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.

nodes.title: Revenue recognition.
nodes.heading: 2.11 Revenue recognition.
nodes.start_phrase: The Company’s revenue from contracts with customers consists of casino wagers transactions, hotel room sales, food and beverage transactions, entertainment shows, and retail transactions.
nodes.summary:
- Long-lived assets impairment: Reviewed when indicators arise. Compare undiscounted future cash flows to carrying value; if insufficient, record impairment based on fair value (typically discounted cash flows). Include remaining construction costs for in-development assets. All impairment losses recorded in operating expenses.
- Capitalized interest: Capitalize interest on major development/construction using project-specific debt or the weighted-average borrowing cost when no specific debt exists. Capitalization stops when a project is substantially complete or development is suspended beyond a brief period.
- Investments in unconsolidated affiliates (equity method): Carrying value adjusted for share of earnings/losses, amortization of basis differences, and capital contributions/distributions. Distributions exceeding equity earnings treated as return of investment and presented as investing cash inflows. Income/losses, gains, and impairments from these investments classified within operating or non-operating income consistent with their nature and alignment with core operations. Impairment evaluated for other-than-temporary declines using DCF analyses and market multiples, considering intent and ability to hold.
- Goodwill and other intangibles: Annual impairment testing in Q4 and interim when warranted; no impairments in 2016–2018. Optional qualitative (“step zero”) assessment considers macro/industry factors, performance, entity-specific events, and prior valuation headroom. Quantitative tests use DCF and market approaches. From Jan 1, 2017, adopted simplified goodwill impairment (no Step 2); impairment equals excess of carrying amount over fair value, capped at recorded goodwill. License rights tested via DCF; trademarks via relief-from-royalty; recognize impairment if fair value < carrying amount.
- Revenue recognition (ASC 606):
  - Casino: Revenue is net win (gaming wins less losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to MGM China promoters/VIP recorded as reductions of casino revenue. Recognized on a portfolio basis by gaming day. Allocate transaction price to discretionary comps at stand‑alone selling price (SSP); third‑party comps recognized as operating expense. Loyalty incentives: allocate portion of net win to points/coupons at SSP (net of breakage), defer and recognize on redemption in the providing department; third‑party redemptions reduce the liability and are settled with the third party.
  - Rooms, food & beverage, retail: Transaction price is net customer amount; recognize when goods/services are transferred (over the stay for rooms; at delivery for F&B and retail). Sales/usage-based taxes excluded. Company may act as agent for certain entertainment shows and OTA-arranged rooms.
  - Bundled packages (e.g., rooms with F&B/entertainment/convention): Allocate revenue to each good/service based on relative SSP determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances.
- Contract and contract-related liabilities: Include (1) outstanding chip liability, (2) loyalty program obligations, and (3) customer advances and other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, room/convention deposits, unpaid wagers). Generally recognized as revenue within a year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities. Activity and balances for 2017–2018 are summarized in a table.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services recognized as revenue when incurred (primarily related to CityCenter).
- Revenue by source: Disaggregated by type (casino, room, F&B, entertainment, retail/other) and geography in a referenced note.

nodes.title: Contract and Contract-Related Liabilities.
nodes.heading: 2.12 Contract and Contract-Related Liabilities.
nodes.start_phrase: There may be a difference between the timing of cash receipts from the customer and the recognition of revenue, resulting in a contract or contract-related liability.
nodes.summary:
- Casino revenue recognition: Transaction price for casino wagers is net win (wins minus losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to gaming promoters/VIP players (e.g., MGM China) reduce casino revenue. Revenue is recognized on a portfolio basis by gaming day.
- Discretionary comps: When wagers include Company-provided discretionary goods/services to incentivize play, revenue is allocated to those items based on their stand-alone selling price (SSP). Comps supplied by third parties are recorded as operating expense.
- Loyalty programs: A portion of net win equal to the SSP of earned incentives (less estimated breakage) is deferred and recognized upon redemption, in the department providing the good/service. Redemptions at third-party outlets reduce the loyalty liability; amounts paid to third parties are settled in cash, and any discount received is recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives to gaming customers totaled $2.3B (2018), $2.1B (2017), and $1.8B (2016). Residual amounts after allocations are recorded as casino revenue.
- Rooms, food & beverage, retail: Transaction price is the net amount collected; revenue is recognized over the hotel stay or upon delivery for F&B and retail. Sales and usage-based taxes are excluded. The Company acts as an agent in certain arrangements (e.g., some entertainment shows and rooms booked via online travel agents).
- Bundled packages: For packages combining rooms with food, beverage, entertainment, or convention services, revenue is allocated to each component based on relative SSP, primarily determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances.
- Contract and contract-related liabilities: Arise from timing differences between cash receipts and revenue recognition and include (1) outstanding chip liability, (2) loyalty program obligations (deferred revenue for incentives), and (3) customer advances and other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, room/convention deposits, unpaid wagers). These are generally recognized as revenue within one year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities.
  - 2018 year-end balances: Outstanding chip liability $323.8M; Loyalty program $113.3M; Customer advances and other $667.3M. Changes in 2018: chip liability decreased $273.9M; loyalty increased $22.2M; customer advances increased $127.7M.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services are recognized as revenue when incurred, primarily related to management of CityCenter.
- Revenue disaggregation: Revenue is presented by source (casino, room, food & beverage, entertainment, retail & other) and by geographic region in a referenced note.

nodes.title: Reimbursed costs.
nodes.heading: 2.13 Reimbursed costs.
nodes.start_phrase: Costs reimbursed pursuant to management services are recognized as revenue in the period it incurs the costs as this reflects when the Company performs its related performance obligation and is entitled to reimbursement.
nodes.summary:
- Defines casino transaction price as net win (gaming wins minus losses); discounts on markers and commissions to gaming promoters/VIP players (e.g., MGM China) reduce casino revenue.
- Recognizes casino revenue on a portfolio basis using net win per gaming day rather than on individual wagers.
- Allocates a portion of casino wager consideration to discretionary comps (goods/services) based on standalone selling price (SSP); comps provided by third parties are recorded as operating expense.
- Loyalty programs: allocates part of net win to loyalty incentives at SSP less estimated breakage; defers and recognizes when redeemed, in the department providing the good/service; third‑party redemptions reduce the loyalty liability and any discount is other revenue.
- Reports commissions and incentives to gaming customers totaling $2.3B (2018), $2.1B (2017), and $1.8B (2016); residual consideration after allocations is recorded as casino revenue.
- Rooms, food & beverage, and retail: transaction price is the net amount collected; revenue recognized over the hotel stay or upon delivery; sales and usage‑based taxes excluded. In some arrangements the Company acts as agent (e.g., certain entertainment shows, OTA‑booked rooms).
- Multi‑element contracts (e.g., packages bundling rooms with F&B or entertainment): revenue allocated to each element based on relative SSP, primarily determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances.
- Contract and contract‑related liabilities include: outstanding chip liability; loyalty program obligations (deferred revenue for earned incentives); and customer advances/other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, deposits for rooms/conventions, unpaid wagers). Generally recognized as revenue within one year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities. A table summarizes 2017–2018 beginning/ending balances and changes for these liabilities.
- Reimbursed costs under management services are recognized as revenue when incurred (primarily related to CityCenter).
- Revenue is disaggregated by source (casino; room; food & beverage; entertainment, retail & other) and by geographic region, as referenced elsewhere in the notes.

nodes.title: Revenue by source.
nodes.heading: 2.14 Revenue by source.
nodes.start_phrase: The Company presents the revenue earned disaggregated by the type or nature of the good or service (casino, room, food and beverage, and entertainment, retail and other) and by relevant geographic region within Note 16.
nodes.summary:
- Casino revenue recognition: Transaction price is net win (gaming wins less losses). Discounts on markers and commissions to promoters/VIP players reduce casino revenue. Revenue is recognized on a portfolio basis per gaming day. For discretionary comps bundled with wagers, revenue is allocated to the goods/services at stand‑alone selling price (SSP); third‑party comps are expensed.
- Loyalty programs: A portion of net win is allocated to loyalty incentives at SSP net of estimated breakage, deferred, and recognized upon redemption in the providing department. Third‑party redemptions reduce the loyalty liability; amounts paid to third parties are expensed with any discount recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives to gaming customers were $2.3B (2018), $2.1B (2017), $1.8B (2016). Residual amounts after allocations are recorded as casino revenue.
- Non-casino revenue (rooms, food & beverage, retail): Transaction price is the net amount collected. Revenue is recognized over the hotel stay or upon delivery of goods/services; sales and usage‑based taxes are excluded. In certain arrangements the Company acts as an agent (e.g., some entertainment shows and rooms sold via online travel agents).
- Bundled contracts: For packages combining rooms with food, beverage, or entertainment, revenue is allocated to each element based on relative SSP, generally determined from standalone pricing in similar circumstances to similar customers.
- Contract and contract‑related liabilities: Three types—outstanding chip liability; loyalty program obligations; and customer advances/other (casino front money, advance ticket sales, deposits on rooms and convention space, unpaid wagers). Generally recognized as revenue within one year and recorded in Other accrued liabilities. Balances: Outstanding chip liability declined to $324M at 12/31/2018 from $598M; loyalty obligations rose to $113M from $91M; customer advances/other rose to $667M from $540M.
- Reimbursed costs: Costs reimbursed under management services are recognized as revenue when incurred (primarily CityCenter management).
- Revenue disaggregation and lease revenues: Revenue is presented by type (casino, room, F&B, entertainment/retail/other) and geography (Note 16). Lease revenues are classified by the tenant’s activity, including F&B lease revenue of $51M (2018, 2017) and $50M (2016), and entertainment/retail/other lease revenue of $87M (2018), $79M (2017), $77M (2016).
- Advertising: Expensed when first run; expense was $305M (2018), $223M (2017), $171M (2016).
- Corporate expense: Unallocated payroll, aircraft, professional fees, and other non‑property costs, including expenses for evaluating/pursuing new business opportunities (expensed as incurred).
- Preopening and start‑up expenses: Expensed as incurred; include payroll, outside services, advertising, and other start‑up costs.
- Property transactions, net: Includes impairments/write‑downs, demolition costs, and gains/losses on asset sales (see Note 15).
- Redeemable noncontrolling interests (MGM National Harbor): Non‑voting interests receive annual preferred distributions based on a percentage of net gaming revenue, accrued quarterly and paid 90 days after year‑end. Beginning 12/31/2019, holders have put rights; certain early sell‑back rights exist if guarantees/liens are granted by the Company. Classified as mezzanine equity; initially recorded at fair value, then adjusted to the maximum redemption value (not below initial) with changes recorded to additional paid‑in capital; carrying amount also adjusted for accrued preferred distributions, which impact net income attributable to noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Advertising.
nodes.heading: 2.15 Advertising.
nodes.start_phrase: The Company expenses advertising costs the first time the advertising takes place.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue presentation: Lease revenues from third-party tenants are recorded within the line item that reflects the tenant’s goods or services (e.g., food and beverage; entertainment, retail, and other). Reported lease revenue amounts: food & beverage—$51m (2018), $51m (2017), $50m (2016); entertainment/retail/other—$87m (2018), $79m (2017), $77m (2016).
- Advertising: Expensed when first run; generally included in general and administrative expenses. Totals: $305m (2018), $223m (2017), $171m (2016).
- Corporate expense: Unallocated costs (payroll, aircraft, professional fees, other) not tied to casino resort operations; includes costs to evaluate/pursue new business opportunities, expensed as incurred.
- Preopening and start-up expenses: Expensed as incurred; include payroll, outside services, advertising, and other costs related to new or start-up operations.
- Property transactions, net: Captures write-downs/impairments, demolition costs, and gains/losses on asset sales; further details referenced in Note 15.
- Redeemable noncontrolling interests (MGM National Harbor): Non-voting economic interests entitled to annual preferred distributions based on a percentage of annual net gaming revenue; distributions accrued quarterly and paid 90 days post fiscal year-end. Beginning Dec 31, 2019, holders can require a purchase of their interests at a formula-based price; certain early sale rights exist if guarantees/liens are granted on non–MGM National Harbor debt. Classified in mezzanine equity (not stockholders’ equity) since redemption is not solely in the Company’s control. Initially recorded at fair value; subsequently adjusted to the maximum redemption value (not below initial carrying value) with changes recorded to additional paid-in capital. Carrying amount also adjusted for accrued preferred distributions, with related changes recognized in net income (loss) attributable to noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Corporate expense.
nodes.heading: 2.16 Corporate expense.
nodes.start_phrase: Corporate expense represents unallocated payroll, aircraft costs, professional fees and various other expenses not directly related to the Company’s casino resort operations.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue classification: Lease revenues from third-party tenants are recorded within the line item matching the tenant’s service (e.g., food and beverage; entertainment, retail, and other). Amounts included: Food and beverage lease revenue of $51 million (2018), $51 million (2017), $50 million (2016); Entertainment, retail, and other lease revenue of $87 million (2018), $79 million (2017), $77 million (2016).
- Advertising costs: Expensed the first time the advertising occurs; generally recorded in general and administrative expenses. Totals were $305 million (2018), $223 million (2017), and $171 million (2016).
- Corporate expense: Unallocated costs such as payroll, aircraft, professional fees, and other corporate items, including costs to evaluate and pursue new business opportunities, expensed as incurred.
- Preopening and start-up expenses: Expensed as incurred; include payroll, outside services, advertising, and other costs related to new or start-up operations.
- Property transactions, net: Classification for write-downs/impairments, demolition costs, and normal gains/losses on asset sales; further detail referenced in Note 15.
- Redeemable noncontrolling interests (MGM National Harbor): Non-voting economic interests receive annual preferred distributions based on a percentage of annual net gaming revenue; accrued quarterly and paid 90 days after fiscal year-end. Beginning December 31, 2019, holders can require MGM National Harbor to purchase their interests per a formula; certain holders can sell earlier if specified guarantees/liens are granted by the Company or affiliates. Classified in mezzanine equity as redemption is not solely within the Company’s control; initially recorded at fair value, subsequently adjusted to the maximum redemption value (not below initial), with changes recorded to additional paid-in capital. Carrying amount also adjusted for accrued preferred distributions, impacting net income attributable to noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Preopening and start-up expenses.
nodes.heading: 2.17 Preopening and start-up expenses.

nodes.summary:

Included amounts: food and beverage lease revenue of $51 million (2018), $51 million (2017), and $50 million (2016); entertainment, retail, and other lease revenue of $87 million (2018), $79 million (2017), and $77 million (2016).
- Advertising: Advertising costs are expensed when first run and recorded primarily in general and administrative expenses. Totals were $305 million (2018), $223 million (2017), and $171 million (2016).
- Corporate expense: Unallocated costs such as payroll, aircraft, professional fees, and other corporate items, including costs to evaluate and pursue new business opportunities, are expensed as incurred.
- Preopening and start-up expenses: Organizational and start-up costs (payroll, outside services, advertising, and related items) are expensed as incurred.
- Property transactions, net: Includes impairments/write-downs, demolition costs, and gains/losses on asset sales; further detail referenced in Note 15.
- Redeemable noncontrolling interest (MGM National Harbor): Noncontrolling parties receive annual preferred distributions based on a percentage of annual net gaming revenue, accrued quarterly and paid 90 days after year-end. Beginning December 31, 2019, holders can require MGM National Harbor to purchase their interests per a formula; certain early sellback rights exist if the Company guarantees or secures other indebtedness. These interests are recorded as redeemable noncontrolling interests (mezzanine), initially at fair value; subsequently adjusted to the maximum redemption value (not below initial), with changes recorded in capital in excess of par. The carrying amount is also adjusted for accrued preferred distributions, with related changes reflected in net income attributable to noncontrolling interests.

nodes.title: Empire City
nodes.heading: 4.2 Empire City
nodes.start_phrase: On January 29, 2019, the Company acquired the real property and operations associated with the Empire City Casino's race track and casino (“Empire City”)for total consideration of approximately $864 million, plus customary working capital and other adjustments (“Empire City Acquisition”).
nodes.summary:
- Empire City acquisition: On January 29, 2019, the Company acquired Empire City Casino’s racetrack and casino for approximately $864 million plus customary adjustments. Consideration included assumption of ~$246 million of debt (subsequently repaid), issuance of ~$266 million in common stock, and the remainder in cash. There is contingent consideration of $50 million if a live table games license is awarded by December 31, 2022 and accepted by December 31, 2024. Preliminary purchase accounting is not yet complete. Post-closing, MGP acquired the developed real property and leases it back to a Company subsidiary.

- Borgata acquisition: On August 1, 2016, the Company acquired Boyd Gaming’s ownership interest in Borgata for $604 million in cash, after which MGP acquired Borgata’s real property and leased it back to a Company subsidiary. Borgata entered into a property tax reimbursement agreement in February 2017 with New Jersey’s Department of Community Affairs and Atlantic City, receiving $72 million in June 2017, half of which was paid to Boyd Gaming net of fees. The transaction resulted in the Company obtaining 100% ownership, consolidating Borgata as of August 1, 2016, and recognizing assets and liabilities at fair value. The pre-existing 50% equity method stake was remeasured, implying a total Borgata equity value of approximately $1.2 billion and a $430 million step-acquisition gain. Borgata’s results from August 1 to December 31, 2016 were: net revenue $350 million, operating income $34 million, and net income $4 million.

- Pro forma information: Unaudited pro forma results assuming control as of January 1, 2015 (excluding the $430 million gain) for the year ended December 31, 2016 show net revenues of $9,963,322 thousand, net income attributable to MGM Resorts International of $818,247 thousand, basic EPS of $1.44, and diluted EPS of $1.43.

nodes.title: Basis Differences

nodes.start_phrase: The Company’s investments in unconsolidated affiliates do not equal the Company’s share of venture-level equity due to various basis differences.

Basis differences tied to depreciable assets are amortized over useful lives; those tied to non‑depreciable assets (e.g., land, indefinite‑lived intangibles) are not amortized.
- Reconciles the Company’s share of venture-level equity to its recorded investment balance for 2018 and 2017, detailing major components:
  - Adjustment to CityCenter equity upon contribution of net assets by MGM Resorts International.
  - CityCenter capitalized interest (including on sponsor notes converted to equity in 2013).
  - CityCenter completion guarantee contributions treated as equity.
  - Deferred gain on assets contributed to CityCenter at formation.
  - Significant other‑than‑temporary impairments of the CityCenter investment, including portions allocated to land.
  - Acquisition fair value adjustments and impairments related to the Grand Victoria investment (applicable in 2017).
  - Other adjustments.
- Presents totals showing the Company’s venture-level equity attributable to it versus the resulting investment balance for each year.

  - Finite‑lived intangible assets primarily include the MGM Grand Paradise gaming subconcession and the MGM Macau land concession, along with customer lists (MGM China, Borgata, and added Northfield in 2018) and other gaming licenses, all presented net of accumulated amortization.

nodes.title: INCOME TAXES
nodes.heading: NOTE 10 — INCOME TAXES
nodes.start_phrase: The Company recognizes deferred income tax assets, net of applicable reserves, related to net operating losses, tax credit carryforwards and certaintemporary differences.
nodes.summary:
- Debt facilities and compliance:
  - MGM China’s credit facility includes standard reps and warranties, events of default, and covenants, including maximum leverage and minimum interest coverage; MGM China was in compliance as of December 31, 2018.

- Parent company senior notes activity:
  - Repaid $850 million 8.625% notes due 2019 in February 2019.
  - Issued $1.0 billion of 5.750% senior notes due 2025 in June 2018.
  - Redeemed $475 million of 11.375% notes due 2018 in July 2017, incurring a $30 million loss on early retirement.

- Operating Partnership senior notes:
  - Issued $350 million of 4.50% notes due 2028 in September 2017.
  - Issued $750 million of 5.75% notes due 2027 in January 2019.
  - Notes are fully and unconditionally guaranteed on a senior basis by certain subsidiaries (other than the co-issuer). Redemption terms include par plus make-whole (if prior to three months before maturity), plus accrued interest. Indentures include customary covenants and events of default, with exceptions including unlimited restricted payments to maintain MGP’s REIT status.

- Long-term debt:
  - Maturity schedule at December 31, 2018 totals $15.253 billion, with principal due by year: 2019 $1.273b; 2020 $1.966b; 2021 $1.716b; 2022 $2.306b; 2023 $2.885b; thereafter $5.107b.
  - Estimated fair value of long-term debt: $15.1 billion (2018) and $13.6 billion (2017), based on quoted market prices.

- Income taxes overview:
  - Deferred tax assets recognized for NOLs, credits, and temporary differences, subject to valuation allowances; benefits recognized when more likely than not.
  - Income (loss) before taxes by geography (2016–2018) presented, showing primarily domestic income and variable foreign results.
  - Detailed tax provision/benefit by federal, state, and foreign components for 2016–2018 and effective tax rate reconciliations, highlighting key drivers such as Tax Act impacts, foreign rates, credits, Macau dividend tax, and valuation allowances.
  - Net deferred tax liability totaled approximately $1.343 billion at December 31, 2018, with major liabilities for property and equipment and intangibles; significant federal/state and foreign deferred tax asset and liability components disclosed.

- U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act) impacts:
  - Summary of major provisions (rate reduction to 21%, transition tax, GILTI, interest and compensation limitations, bonus depreciation, etc.).
  - SAB 118 measurement period applied: recorded a provisional $1.4 billion non-cash net tax benefit in 2017 ($988 million from rate reduction; $438 million from FTC valuation allowance reassessment). No transition tax expense due to FTC offsets.
  - Measurement period finalized in 2018: recorded $20 million non-cash tax expense from FTC-related valuation allowance adjustments and finalized treatment of certain fringe benefits (immaterial).
  - GILTI accounted for as current period expense when incurred; no deferred tax recorded for future GILTI.

- Foreign tax credits (FTCs) and valuation allowances:
  - $2.9 billion FTC carryover as of December 31, 2018, primarily from Macau Special Gaming Tax; $2.4 billion valuation allowance recorded, resulting in a $481 million net FTC deferred tax asset.
  - Expect limited new FTC generation under the Tax Act; utilization dependent on foreign source income and recapture of $1.7 billion overall domestic losses.
  - FTC expirations: $640m (2022), $976m (2023), $782m (2024), $332m (2025), $196m (2027). Significant judgment involved; changes could materially affect the valuation allowance and tax provision.

- Macau tax matters:
  - MGM Grand Paradise’s gaming profits exempt from 12% complementary tax through March 31, 2020. Without the exemption, net income would have decreased by $43 million (2018) and $38 million (2017).
  - Post-March 31, 2020, the company assumes payment of the 12% tax on gaming profits for deferred tax measurement.
  - Non-gaming operations subject to complementary tax; $866 million non-gaming NOL carryforward at December 31, 2018 expiring 2019–2021.
  - Dividend distributions: annual fee arrangement to settle 12% complementary tax on distributions for profits earned through December 31, 2016; extended on March 15, 2018 to cover profits earned January 1, 2017–March 31, 2020 (approximately $1 million per year for 2017–2019 and $0.3 million for Q1 2020). Reversal of previously recorded $41 million deferred tax on 2017 earnings reduced 2018 tax provision, partially offset by the annual payment.

- Other NOLs and valuation allowances:
  - State NOLs of $355 million at December 31, 2018 (DTAs of $23 million), expiring 2029–2038; $3 million valuation allowance on certain state DTAs.
  - $26 million valuation allowance on certain Macau DTAs and $2 million on Hong Kong NOLs.

- Unrecognized tax benefits and audits:
  - Gross unrecognized tax benefits increased to $24.5 million at December 31, 2018; $13 million would affect the effective tax rate if recognized. Interest and penalties immaterial; no material change expected within 12 months.
  - Tax filings across U.S. federal, state, local, and foreign jurisdictions; 2014 U.S. consolidated return under IRS examination. CityCenter’s 2014 IRS exam completed in 2018 with immaterial impact.
  - State exams ongoing: Mississippi and New Jersey (2014–2016), Michigan (2014–2017). Earlier periods generally closed, subject to NOL utilization adjustments.

- Commitments and contingencies:
  - Leases: company leases real estate and equipment under operating and some capital leases, with certain leases including indexed or appraisal-based rent escalations.

nodes.title: October 1 litigation.
nodes.heading: 11.2 October 1 litigation.
nodes.start_phrase: The Company and/or certain of its subsidiaries have been named as defendants in a number of lawsuits related to the October 1, 2017shooting in Las Vegas.
nodes.summary:
- Operating lease commitments: At December 31, 2018, future minimum lease payments totaled $1,702,034 thousand, with scheduled payments of $106,643 (2019), $83,150 (2020), $62,437 (2021), $47,036 (2022), $45,157 (2023), and $1,357,611 thereafter. Obligations under a master lease with a subsidiary are excluded due to consolidation.

- Key lease arrangements:
  - Cotai land concession accounted for as an operating lease; upfront payments amortized over 25 years to January 2038.
  - Borgata: Series of ground leases covering ~11 acres (employee garage, expansions, parking); unfavorable lease liability recognized for above‑market obligations, amortized straight‑line through December 2070; remaining balance $46 million (2018) and $47 million (2017).
  - MGM National Harbor: Ground lease for ~23 acres; initial 25‑year term with up to 13 additional six‑year extensions; first seven options deemed reasonably assured; amortized over a 67‑year term to December 2082.
- October 1, 2017 Las Vegas shooting litigation:
  - Multiple lawsuits filed alleging negligence, seeking damages for emotional distress, injury, medical expenses, economic losses, and wrongful death; cases in Nevada (Clark County) and California (Los Angeles County), with some voluntarily dismissed and anticipated to be refiled.

  - The Company cannot reliably predict outcomes or estimate a range of reasonably possible loss at this time; believes it may incur liability in some cases but expects losses, if any, to be within insurance coverage.

nodes.title: Other litigation.

The settlement was paid in June 2017 via bond proceeds. The company recorded the receipt as an offset to general and administrative (G&A) expenses and, per the 2016 Borgata acquisition terms, paid Boyd Gaming half of the net settlement, recorded in G&A.
- NV Energy exit: The company exited NV Energy’s bundled service in 2016, paying an $83 million upfront impact fee (including $14 million for CityCenter) and initially estimating $71 million for ongoing non-bypassable charges. These were recorded as “NV Energy exit expense” in 2016; subsequent accretion/estimate changes are recorded in G&A. In Q2 2017, obligations were modified to provide a credit and shorten the charge period to 2022, resulting in a $41 million liability reduction (CityCenter: $8 million). As of December 31, 2018 (and 2017), remaining discounted liabilities were $8 million ($10 million) in Other accrued liabilities and $15 million ($23 million) in Other long-term obligations.

Payments totaled $11 million in 2018 and $7 million in 2017 (to Expert Angles Limited). Remaining discounted liability at December 31, 2018 was $36 million in Other long-term obligations.

Facility LC limits: Company $250 million; Operating Partnership $75 million; MGM China $100 million. Initial term began April 25, 2016 for 10 years with four 5-year renewal options; triple-net structure. Landlord has a right of first offer on MGM Springfield.

- Rent mechanics and escalators: Annual rent increased to $770M (from $757M) effective April 1, 2018. Roughly 90% base rent and 10% percentage rent as of Dec 31, 2018. Fixed 2% annual escalators on base rent through the sixth lease year, with potential additional 2% thereafter subject to an adjusted net revenue-to-rent test; percentage rent resets in year six and every five years thereafter based on average net revenue. The lease contains customary covenants; the Company was in compliance as of Dec 31, 2018.

- Subsequent and pending transactions with MGP:
  - Empire City: In Jan 2019, MGP acquired the developed real property for ~$634M; master lease amended to add $50M of annual rent (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); landlord ROFO on certain adjacent undeveloped land if developed and sold.
  - Northfield OpCo: Definitive agreement for the Company to acquire Northfield OpCo from MGP for ~$275M; real estate to be leased under the master lease with a $60M annual rent increase (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); expected close H1 2019.
  - Park MGM Lease Transaction: Agreement for MGP to pay $638M for Park MGM/NoMad Las Vegas renovations; master lease amendment to add $50M annual rent (90% fixed, 2% annual growth until 2022); expected close Q1 2019.

Those MGM subsidiaries keep the real estate on their balance sheets and record finance liabilities (within other long-term obligations) for lease payments and related interest; the same assets also appear on MGP’s balance sheet, with eliminations reflected in consolidating columns.
  - ASC 842 impact: The Company is reassessing whether the master lease transactions now qualify as a sale and the corresponding lease classification, which could affect the condensed consolidating information.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.heading: 8.1 Competition.
nodes.start_phrase: Except as otherwise explicitly provided in Paragraph 10 of this Agreement, during the entireSpecified Term and thereafter for the “Restrictive Period” (defined below in Section 22) Employee shall notdirectly or indirectly be employed by, provide consultation or other services to, engage in, participate in orotherwise be connected in any way with any “Competitor” (defined below in Section 22)
nodes.summary:
- Context: Partial employment agreement for a company engaged in, or applying to engage in, the gaming industry, with heightened regulatory requirements.
- Licensing and regulatory compliance (Sections 6–7):
  - Employee must apply for and obtain any licenses, qualifications, clearances, or approvals required by the Employer or relevant gaming regulators.
  - Employer may terminate employment (per Section 10.1) if: the employee fails to meet licensing requirements; a government authority directs the Employer to cease business with the employee; the Employer believes the employee’s activities could jeopardize its business, reputation, or licenses; or any of the Employer’s licenses are threatened, denied, curtailed, suspended, or revoked due to the employee’s employment or actions.
- Restrictive covenants (Section 8):
  - Non-compete (8.1): During the Specified Term and for a post-employment Restrictive Period (defined in Section 22), the employee may not work for, consult with, or otherwise be connected to a Competitor in a role the same or similar to any role held with the Employer. Exception: if the employee remains at-will after the Specified Term and is later separated for reasons other than Employer’s Good Cause (defined in Section 22), this non-compete does not apply.
  - Non-solicitation and protection of Trade Secrets (8.2): 
    - At all times during and after employment, the employee may not use, access, disclose, or disseminate Company Group Trade Secrets.
    - During employment and for 12 months thereafter, without the Company’s prior written consent, the employee may not: disclose Company Group Business Contacts to Competitors; solicit, induce, or attempt to take away Business Contacts; or approach, solicit, contract with, hire, or entice Business Contacts to end their relationship or employment with the Company Group.
  - Confidentiality (8.3): During and after employment, the employee may not use or disclose Company Group Confidential Information without prior written consent of designated executives (CEO, COO, or General Counsel), with an exception for disclosures required by law or legal process. 
- Definitions referenced but not included: Confidential Information, Restrictive Period, Competitor, Trade Secrets, Business Contacts, Employer’s Good Cause (all in Section 22).

nodes.title: Non-Solicitation
nodes.heading: 8.2 Non-Solicitation.
nodes.start_phrase: At all times during Employee's employment with the Company and at all times thereafter,Employee shall not use, access, disclose, make known to, or otherwise disseminate for personal gain or for thebenefit of a third party (or induce, encourage or assist others in doing any of the foregoing acts) any CompanyGroup "Trade Secrets" (as defined in Section 22) for any purpose whatsoever.
nodes.summary:
- Carve-out from Section 8.1: If the employee continues at-will after the specified term and is then separated by the employer during the restrictive period for any reason other than “Employer’s Good Cause,” Section 8.1 does not apply.
- Non-solicitation (Section 8.2):
  - Ongoing prohibition during employment and thereafter on using, accessing, disclosing, or disseminating Company Group “Trade Secrets” for personal gain or for third parties (as defined in Section 22).
  - During employment and for 12 months after, without the Company’s prior written consent (at the Company’s sole discretion), the employee may not:
    - Disclose Company Group “Business Contacts” (defined in Section 22) to any competitor or its personnel.
    - Call on, solicit, induce to leave, or take away any Business Contacts.
    - Approach, solicit, contract with, or hire any current Business Contacts, or entice any Business Contact to end their relationship or employment with the Company Group.
- Confidentiality (Section 8.3):
  - During and after employment, the employee may not use, disclose, or share any Company Group Confidential Information outside the Company Group without prior written consent of the CEO, COO, or General Counsel (at the Company’s sole discretion).
  - Exception for disclosures required by law or by legal/administrative processes (the text excerpt ends mid-clause).
- Key terms “Trade Secrets” and “Business Contacts” are defined in Section 22.

nodes.title: Confidentiality
nodes.heading: 8.3 Confidentiality.
nodes.start_phrase: At all times during Employee's employment with the Company, and at all times thereafter,Employee shall not, without the prior written consent of the Company’s Chief Executive Officer, ChiefOperating Officer or General Counsel in each and every instance--such consent to be within the Company's sole and absolute discretion--use, disclose or make known to any person, entity or other third party outside of theCompany Group any Confidential Information belonging to Company Group or its individual members.
nodes.summary:
- Carve-out from Section 8.1: If, after the Specified Term ends, the employee continues at-will and is then separated by the employer during the Restrictive Period for any reason other than Employer’s Good Cause (as defined in Section 22), the employee is not subject to Section 8.1.
- Non-solicitation and trade secret protection (Section 8.2):
  - At all times during and after employment, the employee may not use, access, disclose, or disseminate Company Group Trade Secrets for personal gain or for third parties.
  - During employment and for 12 months thereafter, without the Company’s prior written consent (in its sole discretion), the employee may not:
    - Disclose the Company Group’s Business Contacts to any Competitor or its personnel.
    - Call on, solicit, induce to leave, or take away (or attempt to do so) any Business Contacts.
    - Approach, solicit, contract with, or hire any current Business Contacts, or entice them to end their relationship with or employment by the Company Group.
- Confidentiality (Section 8.3):
  - During and after employment, the employee may not use or disclose any Company Group Confidential Information outside the Company Group without prior written consent from the CEO, COO, or General Counsel (in the Company’s sole discretion).
  - Exceptions: disclosures compelled by law or authority (with 10 days’ advance written notice to allow protective measures), information that becomes public without breach, or information received on a non-confidential basis from a lawful source.
- Third-party information (Section 8.4):
  - The employee must strictly maintain the confidentiality of third parties’ confidential/proprietary information received by the Company Group and use it only as required for job duties and consistent with the Company Group’s agreements, during and after employment.
  - No violation if such information is already public through no wrongful act of the employee or others.
- Ownership and handling of confidential information (Section 8.5):
  - Confidential Information and relationships (including Business Contacts) acquired or developed during employment are the Company’s sole and exclusive property, whether or not they qualify as Trade Secrets.
  - The employee may not store, transfer, maintain, copy, duplicate, or possess Confidential Information on any device or in any format except as expressly approved and issued by the Company, and only with the Company’s express written authorization.

nodes.title: Third Party Information
nodes.heading: 8.4 Third Party Information.
nodes.start_phrase: Employee understands and acknowledges that the Company Group has received, andin the future will receive, from third parties, their confidential or proprietary information subject to a duty tomaintain the confidentiality of such information and to use it only for certain limited purposes.
nodes.summary:
- Defines exceptions to confidentiality obligations: disclosure compelled by court, arbitration, mediation, or legislative hearing (with 10 days’ prior written notice to allow the Company to seek protective measures); information that becomes public without the employee’s or others’ breach; and information lawfully received on a non-confidential basis from a source entitled to disclose it.
- Imposes strict duties to protect third-party confidential/proprietary information the Company Group receives: keep in strict confidence during and after employment; use only as necessary for job duties and consistent with agreements with those third parties; no violation if the information is already public through no wrongful act.
- Confirms that Confidential Information acquired or developed during employment—including Business Contacts/Relationships developed while employed—is the sole and exclusive property of the Company, whether or not it qualifies as a trade secret.
- Prohibits, during employment, storing, transferring, maintaining, copying, duplicating, or otherwise possessing Confidential Information on any device or in any format except those expressly approved and issued by the Company, absent express written authorization.

nodes.title: Acknowledgement of Ownership of Confidential Information Property Acquired or Developed During Employment; Non-Transfer
nodes.heading: 8.5 Acknowledgement of Ownership of Confidential Information Property Acquired or Developed During Employment; Non-Transfer.
nodes.start_phrase: Employee understands, agrees, and hereby confirms that Employee's duties andresponsibilities include acquiring Confidential Information and developing Relationships for the benefit ofCompany and, as applicable, Company Group.
nodes.summary:
- Exceptions to confidentiality: Employee may disclose Company Confidential Information if legally compelled (e.g., court, arbitration, mediation, or legislative hearing) with 10 days’ prior written notice to allow the Company to seek protection; if it becomes public without breach; or if received lawfully on a non-confidential basis from a third party.
- Third-party information: Employee must keep third-party confidential/proprietary information received by the Company strictly confidential, use it only for permitted purposes during and after employment, and is not liable if the information is already publicly known through no wrongful act.
- Ownership of information and relationships: All Confidential Information and business relationships acquired or developed during employment are the Company’s exclusive property, whether or not they qualify as trade secrets.
- Restrictions on storage/transfer: Employee may not store, copy, transfer, or maintain Confidential Information on any device or in any format unless the device is Company-issued or the action is expressly pre-approved in writing by the Company. A wide range of personal devices and media are expressly covered.
- Return and deletion on separation: Upon termination, Employee must immediately return all Confidential Information, retain no copies, delete any such data from all devices, and, upon request, allow the Company to inspect devices and reasonably access personal computers, email accounts, and devices to verify deletion and non-possession.
- Copyright in compilations: The Company owns copyrights in all compilations of Confidential Information (in any medium). Unauthorized copying, distribution, or derivative works constitute infringement. Only the CEO, COO, President, or General Counsel can authorize such use, and authorization must be in writing in advance. Employee agrees not to challenge the Company’s rights and waives defenses.

nodes.title: Return of Confidential Information
nodes.heading: 8.6 Return of Confidential Information.
nodes.start_phrase: Upon termination of Employee's employment for any reason at any time,Employee shall immediately return to the Company, and retain no copies of, any all Confidential Information inEmployee's possession or control.
nodes.summary:
- Prohibits employees from texting, copying, or transferring Confidential Information to any non-company-issued device or storage medium unless expressly pre-approved in writing by the company.
- Broadly defines “Devices” to include computers, phones (including smartphones), tablets, external drives, flash/thumb/zip drives, and similar data storage tools.
- Requires immediate return of all Confidential Information upon termination, with no copies retained; mandates deletion of any such information from all devices and allows company inspection to verify deletion.
- Grants the company reasonable access to employees’ personal computers, email accounts, and devices to confirm no Confidential Information is retained contrary to the agreement.
- Affirms company ownership of copyrights in compilations of Confidential Information (e.g., lists, spreadsheets, databases) in any form or medium.
- States that unauthorized copying, distribution, or creation of derivative works from these compilations constitutes copyright infringement.
- Limits authorization to copy, distribute, or create derivative works to written, advance approvals by the CEO, COO, President, or General Counsel.
- Notes potential civil and criminal penalties for infringement and includes the employee’s agreement not to challenge the company’s rights and to waive defenses.

nodes.title: Acknowledgement of Copyrights in and to Compilations of Confidential Information
nodes.heading: 8.7 Acknowledgement of Copyrights in and to Compilations of Confidential Information.
nodes.start_phrase: Employeeacknowledges that Company owns copyrights in any and all compilations of Confidential Information in anytangible or electronic form (including, but not limited to, printed lists, handwritten lists, spreadsheets, anddatabases) in any storage media, including, but not limited to, Devices, (collectively, “CopyrightedWorks”).

nodes.title: Representations and Warranties
nodes.heading: 9. Representations and Warranties.

nodes.title: Irreparable harm
nodes.start_phrase: Employee acknowledges that the Company has and will continue to invest substantial time and expense indeveloping and protecting Confidential Information, all of which Employee expressly understands and agreesbelongs solely and exclusively to Company.
nodes.summary:
- Employee representations and warranties: acknowledges that part of compensation is tied to agreeing that the restrictive covenants (Sections 4 and 8) are reasonable in scope, duration, and content; agrees not to challenge their reasonableness; agrees they survive termination; and agrees they are freely assignable by the Company in connection with sales, reorganizations, or similar control/ownership changes.
- Employee affirms that enforcement of remedies will not prevent earning a livelihood, given the ability to find work notwithstanding the Section 8 restrictions.
- Employee agrees that the covenants in Sections 4, 6, 7, and 8 are essential to protect the Company’s trade secrets, business contacts, and confidential information, and that the Company has relied on these covenants and representations.
- Employee warrants authority to enter the agreement and perform duties without violating any other agreements or obligations.
- Acknowledgment of the Company’s substantial investment in confidential information; any breach or threatened breach of Sections 4 or 8 would cause irreparable harm, entitling the Company to immediate injunctive relief without posting bond, and Employee agrees not to contest enforceability of such injunctions where lawful.
- Termination—Employer’s Good Cause (defined in Section 22): Employer may terminate during the Specified Term; no further obligations except:
  - If due to Employee’s death: beneficiary receives six months of salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
  - If due to Disability (defined in Section 22): Employee (or beneficiary if Employee dies during the payout period) receives six months of salary, paid at regular intervals, reduced by any Employer-funded short-term disability benefits.
- Termination—Employer’s No Cause: Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term, including the last day, for any or no reason; Employer’s liability is limited to amounts described in provisions that follow (details not included in the excerpt).

nodes.title: Termination
nodes.heading: 10. Termination.
nodes.start_phrase: Employer has the right to terminate this Agreement at anytime during the Specified Term hereof for “Employer’s Good Cause” (defined below in Section 22).
nodes.summary:
- Breach of covenants: A breach or threatened breach of Sections 4 and 8 would cause the Company irreparable harm. The Employee agrees the Company may obtain immediate injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction without posting a bond and without waiving any claim for damages.
- Enforcement: The Employee agrees not to contest the enforceability of such an injunction in any jurisdiction where injunctions are lawful.
- Termination (Section 10): Sets out the Employer’s termination rights and related obligations.
- Employer’s Good Cause Termination (10.1): Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term for “Employer’s Good Cause” (defined in Section 22); upon such termination, the Employer has no further obligations except as in 10.1.1 and 10.1.2.
- Death benefit (10.1.1): If termination for Good Cause results from the Employee’s death, the designated beneficiary receives six months of the Employee’s salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
- Disability benefit (10.1.2): If termination for Good Cause results from the Employee’s “Disability” (defined in Section 22), the Employer pays six months of salary after termination (to the Employee, or to the beneficiary if the Employee dies during the payout period), reduced by any short‑term disability payments under an Employer-funded policy, paid at regular payroll intervals.
- No Cause Termination (10.2): Employer may terminate on written notice, in its sole discretion, for any or no reason at any time during the Specified Term (including the last day). The Employer’s sole liability upon such termination will be as specified in subsequent provisions (not included in this excerpt).

nodes.title: Employer’s Good Cause Termination
nodes.heading: 10.1 Employer’s Good Cause Termination.
nodes.start_phrase: Employer has the right to terminate this Agreement at anytime during the Specified Term hereof for “Employer’s Good Cause” (defined below in Section 22).
nodes.summary:
- Injunctive relief: If the employee breaches or threatens to breach Sections 4 or 8, the company may seek immediate injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction without posting a bond and without waiving any claim for damages. The employee agrees not to contest the enforceability of such injunctions where lawful.
- Termination (Section 10):
  - Employer’s Good Cause Termination (definitions in Section 22): Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term for “Good Cause,” with no further obligations except as noted.
    - Death (10.1.1): If termination is due to the employee’s death, the designated beneficiary receives six months of the employee’s salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
    - Disability (10.1.2): If termination is due to “Disability,” the employer pays six months of salary at regular intervals, reduced by any employer-funded short-term disability payments; if the employee dies during this period, payments continue to the beneficiary.
  - Employer’s No Cause Termination (10.2): Employer may terminate at any time, including the last day of the Specified Term, for any or no reason upon written notice; employer’s sole liability is limited as set forth in conditions referenced but not included in the excerpt.

nodes.title: Death
nodes.start_phrase: In the event Employer’s Good Cause termination is the result of Employee’s death during theSpecified Term, Employee’s beneficiary (as designated by Employee on Employer’s benefit records)shall be entitled to receive Employee’s salary for a six (6) month period following Employee’sdeath, such amount to be paid at regular payroll intervals.
nodes.summary:
- Breach and injunctive relief: A breach or threatened breach of Sections 4 or 8 would cause the Company irreparable harm. The Company is entitled to immediate injunctive relief in a competent court without posting a bond or waiving damages, and the Employee agrees not to contest the injunction’s enforceability where lawful.

- Termination (Section 10):
  - Employer’s Good Cause Termination (defined in Section 22): Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term. Upon such termination, Employer has no further obligations except as below.
    - If termination is due to Employee’s death: Employee’s designated beneficiary receives six months of salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
    - If termination is due to Employee’s Disability (defined in Section 22): Employee (or beneficiary, if Employee dies during the payout period) receives six months of salary at regular intervals, offset by amounts paid from any Employer-funded short-term disability policy.
  - Employer’s No Cause Termination: Employer may terminate on written notice, at its sole discretion, for any or no reason at any time during the Specified Term, including the last day. Employer’s sole liability upon such termination will be as specified in subsequent conditions (not included in the excerpt).

nodes.title: Disability
nodes.start_phrase: In the event Employer’s Good Cause termination is the result of Employee’s “Disability” (definedbelow in Section 22), Employer shall pay Employee (or Employee’s beneficiary in the event ofEmployee’s death during the period in which payments are being made) an amount equal toEmployee’s salary for six (6) months following Employee’s termination, such amount to be paid atregular payroll intervals, net of payments received by Employee from any short term disabilitypolicy which is either self-insured by Employer or the premiums of which were paid by Employer(and not charged as compensation to Employee).
nodes.summary:
- Breach/Threatened Breach Remedies (Sections 4 and 8):
  - Company deems breaches to cause irreparable harm.
  - Company entitled to immediate injunctive relief without posting bond and without waiving damages.
  - Employee agrees not to contest enforceability of such injunctions where lawful.

- Termination (Section 10):
  - 10.1 Employer’s Good Cause Termination (as defined in Section 22):
    - Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term.
    - No further liability to Employee except:
      - 10.1.1 Death: Employee’s designated beneficiary receives six months of salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
      - 10.1.2 Disability (as defined in Section 22): Employee (or beneficiary if Employee dies during payout) receives six months of salary, paid at regular payroll intervals, net of any short-term disability benefits paid under an employer-funded policy.
  - 10.2 Employer’s No Cause Termination:
    - Employer may terminate at any time during the Specified Term, including on the last day, with written notice, for any or no cause.
    - Employer’s sole liability upon such termination is subject to conditions set forth later (details not included in this excerpt).

nodes.title: Employer’s No Cause Termination
nodes.heading: 10.2 Employer’s No Cause Termination.
nodes.start_phrase: Employer has the right to terminate this Agreement on written notice toEmployee in its sole discretion for any cause Employer deems sufficient or for no cause, at any time during theSpecified Term, including on the last day of the Specified Term.
nodes.summary:
- Injunctive relief for breaches: If the employee violates Sections 4 or 8, the company may seek immediate injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction without posting a bond and without waiving damages; the employee agrees not to contest enforceability of such injunction where lawful.
- Termination framework (Section 10):
  - Employer’s Good Cause Termination (as defined in Section 22): Employer may terminate at any time during the specified term; no further obligations except:
    - Death: Beneficiary receives six months of the employee’s salary, paid at regular payroll intervals.
    - Disability (as defined in Section 22): Employee (or beneficiary, if applicable) receives six months of salary, offset by employer-funded short-term disability benefits, paid at regular intervals.
  - Employer’s No Cause Termination: Employer may terminate for any or no reason during the specified term; payments limited to:
    - Severance Payment: Equal to one year of base salary plus Target Bonus (capped at $4,000,000), less taxes, paid in 12 monthly installments starting 30 days after separation; plus any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus under the applicable program.
    - COBRA Payment: Amount equal to 1.5 times the cost of 12 months of COBRA coverage, paid in 12 monthly installments beginning at separation.
    - Special rules:
      - If terminated within six months of hire: Only six months of base salary is payable; the Restrictive Period is limited to six months.
      - If employed at-will after the specified term and then separated for No Cause during the Restrictive Period: Lump sum equal to the greater of 13 weeks of base salary or two times what the employee would receive under the then-effective discretionary severance policy.
  - Release condition: Eligibility for Severance and COBRA Payments requires the employee to execute (and not revoke) within 21 days (or a shorter lawful period) a comprehensive release prepared by the employer, waiving all known and unknown claims related to employment or its cessation against the company and its affiliates.

nodes.title: Severance Payment and COBRA Payment
nodes.start_phrase: Employee shall receive an amount equal to: (i) Employee’s annual base salary and (ii) TargetBonus (the “Severance Payment”) (subject to a maximum Severance Payment of $ 4 million) , less all applicable taxes, payable in twelve (12) monthly installments commencing upon the date that isthirty (30) days after the date of separation; plus any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus due toEmployee, payable in accordance with the provisions of the Program.
nodes.summary:
- Defines severance benefits upon separation, including:
  - Severance Payment equal to (i) one year of base salary plus (ii) Target Bonus, capped at $4,000,000, less taxes, paid in 12 monthly installments starting 30 days after separation.
  - Payment of any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus per the applicable program.
  - COBRA Payment equal to 1.5 times the cost of 12 months of COBRA coverage, paid in 12 monthly installments starting upon separation.
- Special scenarios:
  - If termination occurs within six months of hire: employee receives only six months of base salary; the restrictive period is limited to six months.
  - If the employee continues at-will employment after the specified term and is separated without cause during the restrictive period: a lump-sum payment (less taxes) equal to the greater of (i) 13 weeks of base salary or (ii) two times what the employee would receive under the then-effective discretionary severance policy.
- Eligibility condition:
  - Receipt of Severance and COBRA Payments is expressly conditioned on the employee signing (within 21 days of termination or a shorter lawful period) and not revoking a company-prepared release waiving all known and unknown claims against the company, its affiliates, and related parties, covering claims arising from employment or its cessation, including those under employment agreements, tort, compensation and benefits (salary, bonus, stock, PTO, insurance), and applicable state and federal laws.

nodes.title: Release requirement
nodes.start_phrase: Employee’s eligibility for the Severance Payment and COBRA Payment set forth in Section 10.2.1shall be expressly subject to, conditioned upon, and in consideration of Employee’s execution,within twenty-one (21) days following the date of Employee’s termination of employment (or suchshorter time period as may be required by the Company consistent with applicable law) and non-revocation of a release prepared by Employer and waiving and releasing Employer and theCompany,
nodes.summary:
- Severance payments upon separation:
  - Base severance equals one year of base salary plus target bonus, capped at $4,000,000, less applicable taxes, paid in 12 monthly installments starting 30 days after separation.
  - Any earned but unpaid discretionary bonus is also payable per the applicable bonus program.
  - COBRA Payment equal to 1.5 times the cost of 12 months of COBRA coverage, paid in 12 monthly installments beginning at separation.

- Special severance scenarios:
  - If termination occurs within six months of hire: severance limited to six months of base salary; Restrictive Period shortened to six months.
  - If employment continues at-will after the Specified Term and the employee is then separated during the Restrictive Period for No Cause: a lump-sum payment equal to the greater of (i) 13 weeks of base salary or (ii) two times the amount otherwise payable under the company’s then-effective discretionary severance policy.

- Conditions to receive severance/COBRA payments:
  - Employee must execute (within 21 days of termination, or a shorter lawful period set by the company) and not revoke a company-prepared release of claims.
  - The release broadly waives known and unknown claims related to employment or its cessation, including statutory, contract, tort, wage/benefit, and discrimination claims under federal, state, and local laws (e.g., Title VII, ADEA/OWBPA, ADA, EPA, FMLA, ERISA, GINA, WARN, NLRA, Nevada statutes), and becomes irrevocable within 30 days or fewer after termination.

- Ongoing obligations and consequences:
  - Post-termination cooperation: employee must reasonably assist with matters they worked on and with ongoing/future legal matters related to their role.

nodes.title: Defend Trade Secrets Act Notice
