nodes.title: Exhibit B - Arbitration
nodes.heading: EXHIBIT B - AR B I TRATION
nodes.start_phrase: This Exhibit B sets forth the methods for resolving any controversy, dispute or claim directly or indirectly arising out of orrelating to the Employment Agreement (“Agreement”), or the breach thereof, or arising out of or relating to the employmentof Employee, or the termination thereof,
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Establishes binding arbitration as the exclusive method (with limited exceptions) to resolve any controversy, dispute, or claim arising out of or relating to the Employment Agreement, the employee’s employment, or its termination. Becomes part of the Employment Agreement.
- Covered claims: Broadly covers statutory, contractual, tort, and common-law employment claims, including discrimination, harassment, wrongful termination, wage and hour, FMLA, ADA, ADEA, Title VII, Section 1981–1988, FLSA, GINA, Nevada employment and civil rights laws, whistleblower, and public policy claims, as well as disputes over compensation, terms, and conditions of employment, and pre-employment statements/actions.
- Parties covered: Applies to claims against the employer, its officers, directors, employees, agents, subsidiaries, divisions, affiliates, successors, and assigns.
- Class/representative action waiver: Employee has no right to bring or arbitrate claims as a class, collective, representative, or private attorney general action.
- Agency filings: Does not preclude filing charges with agencies (e.g., EEOC, NLRB); however, employee waives participation in monetary or other recovery in third-party actions for claims subject to this arbitration agreement.
- Excluded claims: Workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance claims; claims related to employee welfare benefit and pension plans (must use plan procedures); and injunctive or other relief for non-competition and confidentiality violations by either party.
- Non-waiver of substantive rights: Substantive statutory and common-law rights and remedies remain intact; only the judicial forum is waived.
- Time limits and notice: Arbitration must be initiated within the applicable statute of limitations. Written notice describing the claim, facts, and relief sought must be provided within that time frame (to the Employer’s President with a copy to MGM Resorts International’s EVP & General Counsel, or to the employee’s last known address if the employer is the aggrieved party).
- Arbitration forum and selection: Administered by JAMS under its then-current employment arbitration rules. Arbitrator must be a retired judge or experienced employment attorney licensed in the state of arbitration. Selection from a JAMS list of seven neutrals; if no agreement, each party strikes one name and the remaining arbitrator is selected.
- Governing law and procedures: Nevada substantive law (and remedies law), and applicable federal law, govern. Arbitrator cannot apply different substantive law. Non-economic or punitive damages only if authorized by applicable law, with citation required. Privileges apply. Reasonable discovery permitted (written, depositions, subpoenas), disputes on scope decided by arbitrator. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment allowed. Federal Rules of Evidence used. Witness lists exchanged 30 days before hearing; subpoena power available; optional court reporter at a party’s expense. Hearings are private; venue is Las Vegas, Nevada, unless the employee works outside Clark County, in which case venue is in the employee’s county and state of employment.
- Award: Written decision with issues, findings of fact, and conclusions of law; typically issued within 30 days after the hearing or post-hearing briefs. Relief cannot exceed what a court could grant. Award is final and binding; judgment may be entered in court.
- Court involvement: Either party may go to court to compel arbitration or to confirm, enforce, vacate, or modify an award as permitted by law.
- Fees and costs: Employer pays any filing fee and arbitrator’s fees/costs. Each party bears its own attorneys’ fees and litigation expenses, except where a statute or written agreement authorizes fee/cost shifting, in which case the arbitrator may award them under the applicable legal standards.
- Survival and modification: Arbitration provisions survive termination of employment and expiration of the Agreement; they may be modified or revoked only by a signed writing expressly stating that intent.
- No effect on termination provisions: Arbitration terms do not alter the Agreement’s termination provisions. Capitalized terms have the meanings in the Employment Agreement. Severability preserves remaining provisions if any part is unenforceable.
- Acknowledgment: Both parties confirm they have read and understand Exhibit B, agree it is a material employment term, and voluntarily waive a judicial forum (court or jury) for covered claims, without waiving substantive rights. Employee acknowledges the opportunity to consult private legal counsel.
- Signatories indicated: Employee (John M. McManus) and Employer (MGM Resorts International, by James J. Murren, Chairman and CEO).

The list also covers the real estate/REIT platform MGM Growth Properties and its GP, operating partnership, finance co-issuer, and lessor entities. International subsidiaries reflect hospitality, branding, marketing, and gaming footprints across Hong Kong, Macau, Mainland China (Beijing), Singapore, India, Japan, Dubai, Isle of Man, Cayman Islands, and the British Virgin Islands, including MGM China Holdings and MGM Asia Pacific. Additional subsidiaries manage arenas and entertainment venues (Las Vegas Arena Management, Park Theater, Grand Garden Arena Management), interactive gaming and sports betting, aviation, manufacturing, insurance, laundry, and retail. Jurisdictions prominently include Nevada, Delaware, Massachusetts, Mississippi, New York, New Jersey, Ohio, and multiple offshore financial and operational hubs. Overall, the exhibit demonstrates MGM’s vertically integrated structure across operations, development, branding, international expansion, and real estate financing.

nodes.title: Exhibit 99.1 Description of Our Operating Resorts
nodes.heading: Exhibit 99.1 DESCRIPTION OF OUR OPERATING RESORTS
nodes.start_phrase: The following information des cribes each of our operating resorts, including their key amenities, features and awards.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose: Exhibit 99.1 provides an overview of the company’s operating resorts, highlighting locations, awards, signature amenities, dining, entertainment, retail, meeting/convention space, and unique attractions.

- Las Vegas Strip portfolio:
  - Bellagio: AAA Five Diamond; iconic fountains and seasonal conservatory; fine dining (Picasso, Le Cirque); spa, pool, Gallery of Fine Art; Via Bellagio luxury retail; Cirque du Soleil’s “O”; connections to Vdara and Crystals.
  - MGM Grand Las Vegas: AAA Four Diamond; StayWell rooms, Skylofts (AAA Five Diamond), The Mansion; The Signature all‑suite non‑gaming; celebrity dining (including Joël Robuchon, Michelin three‑star); entertainment (KÀ by Cirque du Soleil, MGM Grand Garden Arena, David Copperfield, Brad Garrett’s Comedy Club); nightlife (Hakkasan, Wet Republic); extensive meeting space and trade show pavilion; wedding chapel, pool/spa.
  - Mandalay Bay: AAA Four Diamond; restaurants by noted chefs; multiple venues (12,000‑seat arena, House of Blues, Michael Jackson ONE by Cirque); 2.1M sq ft of convention space; Shark Reef Aquarium; expansive beach/pool complex with concerts, Moorea and Daylight Beach Club; Spa Mandalay; includes Four Seasons (AAA Five Diamond) and Delano (with Rivea and Skyfall by Alain Ducasse).
  - The Mirage: AAA Four Diamond; erupting volcano, tropical atrium; Secret Garden and Dolphin Habitat; dining; entertainment (The Beatles LOVE by Cirque, Terry Fator, Aces of Comedy); nightlife (1OAK, Parlor); retail and 170,000 sq ft of meetings/convention space.
  - Luxor: Pyramid with signature light beam; meeting space, spa; dining (TENDER, Public House, Diablo’s Cantina); attractions (Titanic: The Artifact Exhibition, Bodies…The Exhibition); shows (Blue Man Group, Carrot Top, Fantasy).
  - Excalibur: Castle‑themed; shows (Tournament of Kings, The Australian Bee Gees, Thunder from Down Under); attractions (Fun Dungeon arcade, Castle Walk); multiple dining venues; fitness/spa and large pool deck; tram connection to Luxor and Mandalay Bay.
  - New York‑New York: NYC‑themed skyline, roller coaster; dining (Tom’s Urban, Shake Shack, Nine Fine Irishmen); entertainment (Zumanity by Cirque, Times Square piano bar); connected to Park MGM and T‑Mobile Arena via The Park.
  - Park MGM (with NoMad): Dining (Bavette’s, Primrose) and Eataly market; Park Theater (5,200 seats) for headliners; NoMad Hotel features boutique hospitality and Jacques Garcia design.

- Additional U.S. resorts:
  - Circus Circus Las Vegas: Adventuredome indoor theme park, Midway; THE Steak House; Splash Zone water amenities.
  - MGM Grand Detroit: Downtown integrated resort; dining (Wolfgang Puck Steak, TAP); nightlife, spa; 30,000 sq ft of meeting space.
  - Beau Rivage (Biloxi): Beachfront; remodeled rooms; multiple restaurants/bars; 1,550‑seat theatre; upscale retail promenade; spa/salon; 50,000 sq ft of convention space.
  - Gold Strike Tunica: Dockside casino near Memphis; Millennium Theatre; dining; 20,000 sq ft meeting space; part of a three‑casino complex.
  - Borgata (Atlantic City): Extensive gaming; restaurants (Angeline, Bobby Flay Steak, Izakaya, Wolfgang Puck); retail; spa; ~70,000 sq ft of meeting space; Water Club (18,000 sq ft events); Music Box (1,000 seats).
  - MGM National Harbor (MD/DC): Boutique hotel; celebrity chef dining (José Andrés, Voltaggio brothers); 3,000‑seat theater; seasonal conservatory; bars/lounges; 27,000‑sq‑ft spa/salon; curated retail (incl. SJP boutique).
  - MGM Springfield (MA): Downtown resort with locally inspired design; chef‑driven restaurants; lounges; cinema and bowling; spa, pool; 34,000 sq ft of convention space; manages adjacent MassMutual Center (8,000 seats; 100,000 sq ft meetings).

- Macau properties:
  - MGM Macau: Five‑star integrated resort on Macau Peninsula; Grande Praça atrium; rooms/suites/villas; diverse dining; pool/spa; direct connection to One Central luxury retail.
  - MGM Cotai: Award‑winning integrated resort on the Cotai Strip; rooms/suites; meeting space; spa; retail; F&B; The Mansion luxury experience; Asia’s first dynamic theater and innovative spectacle.

- Common themes across properties: industry recognitions (AAA, Michelin), Cirque du Soleil and headline entertainment, celebrity chef dining, expansive meeting/convention facilities, luxury spas and pools, distinctive retail, and unique, destination‑defining attractions with inter‑property connectivity in Las Vegas.

nodes.title: Exhibit 99.2 Description of Regulation and Licensing
nodes.heading: Exhibit 99.2 DESCRIPTION OF REGULATION AND LICENSING
nodes.start_phrase: The gaming industry is highly regulated, and we must maintain our licenses and pay gaming taxes to continue our operations.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The document outlines the extensive regulatory and licensing framework governing a gaming company’s operations across multiple jurisdictions. It stresses the need to maintain licenses, comply with broad legal regimes (e.g., alcohol, smoking, environmental, labor/immigration, tax, zoning/building, marketing/advertising, privacy/telemarketing, OFAC, FCPA, AML), and notes that changes in laws or interpretations could adversely affect results. Violations in one jurisdiction can trigger actions in others.

- Nevada:
  - Oversight by Nevada Gaming Commission, Nevada Gaming Control Board, and local authorities; policies focus on excluding unsuitable persons, robust accounting/internal controls, anti-fraud, accurate reporting, and ensuring tax/licensing revenues.
  - Casino and manufacturer/distributor subsidiaries must be licensed; parent entities registered as publicly traded corporations with detailed reporting.
  - Suitability investigations required for officers, directors, key employees, and certain owners; thresholds include reporting at >5% and suitability at >10%, with institutional investor waivers for investment-only holdings (generally up to 25% and under certain conditions up to 29%).
  - Broad approval/reporting requirements for financings, securities offerings (3-year prior approval granted in 2017), and changes of control; regulation of corporate defensive tactics and extraordinary repurchases.
  - Taxes/fees include a 6.75% tax on gross gaming revenue and a live entertainment tax; foreign gaming revolving fund and conduct standards; alcohol sales licensed and regulated locally.
  - Sanctions for violations range from fines to license limitation/suspension/revocation and possible appointment of a supervisor.

- Michigan (MGM Grand Detroit):
  - Regulated by the Michigan Gaming Control Board; extensive suitability for applicants, affiliates, key persons, and certain owners (with institutional investor exemptions); supplier and occupational licensing requirements.
  - One-year casino license terms with renewal; Board powers include fines, suspension, revocation, and conservatorship.
  - Administrative rules cover investigations/hearings, recordkeeping, internal controls, surveillance, patron credit, and ownership transfers.
  - Share acquisitions >5% require approval; institutional investors may receive waivers under defined thresholds; notification and filings (e.g., 13D/13G) required.
  - Liquor control by the Michigan Liquor Control Commission; Detroit ordinance requires compliance with a development agreement, with potential license revocation upon termination.
  - Prior approval required for debt transactions affecting capitalization/viability.
  - Taxes/fees: 19% wagering tax (shared by state and Detroit), municipal service fee (greater of $4M or 1.25% of adjusted gross receipts), annual state assessment (~$8.3M, CPI-adjusted), and 1%–2% of adjusted gross receipts to Detroit based on revenue thresholds.

- Mississippi (Beau Rivage, Gold Strike Tunica):
  - Oversight by the Mississippi Gaming Commission and Department of Revenue; objectives mirror Nevada (suitability, internal controls, anti-fraud, tax collection, local employment).
  - Gaming permitted in certain counties; post-Katrina law allows land-based facilities on the Gulf Coast within 800 feet of the high-water line; unlimited stakes and number of licenses.
  - Licenses (non-transferable) for up to three years; parent registered as a publicly traded holding company with periodic reporting.
  - Suitability for officers, directors, key employees, and owners (>5% reporting; >10% findings), with institutional investor waivers (investment-only up to 25%/29%).
  - Ability to require suitability of debt holders; restrictions and required actions regarding unsuitable persons (e.g., bar dividends, voting, remuneration; forced divestiture).
  - Maintenance of in-state stockholder records; legend requirement on securities waived in 2009.
  - Approvals/reporting for financings and securities offerings (2015 waiver for prior approval subject to conditions); restrictions on pledges/guarantees and transfers; prior approval for changes of control and certain defensive tactics; foreign gaming approvals.
  - Sanctions include fines, license limitation/suspension/revocation, and possible supervisor appointment; violations by affiliates may impact licensees.
  - Taxes/fees: state fee generally 8% of gross revenue (creditable against state income tax) plus local fee of approximately 4%; infrastructure requirements (parking and amenities) with grandfathering; alcohol service licensed by state and local authorities with 24-hour service in special resort areas and licensing of key officers/owners.

- Macau SAR (MGM Grand Paradise; MGM Macau and MGM Cotai):
  - Gaming operator subject to Macau law and ongoing regulatory scrutiny; government approval required for ownership interests, transfers/encumbrances of shares and voting rights, recapitalizations, and constitutional changes; no delegation of gaming management.
  - Suitability required for shareholders with ≥5%, directors, and key employees; obligation to sever ties with unsuitable persons; prior approval for changes of control.
  - Operator obligations include fair/honest gaming free from criminal influence, hiring qualified personnel, and safeguarding tax revenues; reporting and minimum insurance required.
  - Subconcession governs MGM Macau and MGM Cotai; excludes certain gaming types; Macau law and courts have exclusive jurisdiction.
  - Subconcession expires March 31, 2020; government may redeem with one year’s notice (compensation based on prior-year revenue) or unilaterally terminate for fundamental non-compliance.
  - Taxes/fees: annual premium (fixed plus variable per table/machine with a minimum), 35% special gaming tax on gross gaming revenue plus 1.6% and 2.4% levies; GGR tax not reduced for credit losses.
  - Land concessions: MGM Macau to 2031; MGM Cotai to 2038; premiums paid and annual rents due (subject to five-year reviews).
  - Corporate income tax exemption on gaming profits granted/extended through March 31, 2020.

- Maryland (MGM National Harbor):
  - Regulation of video lottery terminals and table games by the Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Commission and Agency; facility siting by the Maryland Location Commission.
  - MGM National Harbor was found qualified, awarded the sixth and final license, and received an operating license on December 7, 2016 with an initial 15-year term.

nodes.title: Maryland Government Regulation
nodes.heading: Maryland Government Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: The Maryland State Lottery Video Lottery Terminal Law (“Maryland VLT Law”) subjects the owners and operators of video lottery facilities to extensive state licensing and regulatory requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Macau operations (MGM Grand Paradise Limited):
  - Annual concession premium with fixed portion (30 million patacas) plus variable portion per gaming table/machine, subject to a 45 million patacas minimum.
  - Special gaming tax of 35% of gross gaming revenue, plus applicable withholding taxes, and additional levies of 1.6% and 2.4% of gross gaming revenue to designated public foundations and the Macau S.A.R.
  - Gross gaming revenue tax base excludes credit loss deductions; taxes may be due on winnings tied to uncollected markers.
  - Land concessions:
    - MGM Macau: 10.67 acres; concession expires April 6, 2031 (renewable). Premium paid upfront; annual rent subject to review every five years under Macau Land Law.
    - MGM Cotai: ~18 acres; concession expires January 8, 2038 (renewable). Premium paid upfront; annual rent subject to five-year reviews.
  - Corporate income tax exemption in Macau on casino game profits: initial five years from January 1, 2007; extended in 2011 for five years; further extended on September 7, 2016 through March 31, 2020.

- Maryland regulation (MGM National Harbor):
  - Subject to Maryland State Lottery Video Lottery Terminal Law (VLT Law).
  - Regulatory bodies: Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Commission and Agency regulate video lottery terminals and table games; Facility Location Commission awards up to six licenses.
  - Licensing:
    - MGM National Harbor awarded sixth and final video lottery operation license (qualified October 10, 2013; awarded December 23, 2013; operational license issued December 7, 2016) with an initial 15-year term.
    - Initial fee based on 3,600 proposed terminals: $21 million; reapplication allowed within one year of term end for a 10-year license (fee set by statute).
    - Authorized terminals temporarily reduced multiple times (2016–2019); as of December 8, 2019, authorized count set between 3,130 and 3,600, equal to actual operating terminals on that date.
  - Operational rules: minimum 87% average payout per terminal; open 24/7; 21+ age requirement; alcohol cannot be free; restrictions on check cashing, cards, ATMs, and similar transactions.
  - Suitability and ownership:
    - Background investigations for licensees and owners of 5%+ interests; institutional investor waiver available at Commission’s discretion.
    - Ongoing regulation includes possible suspension, revocation, restrictions, civil penalties; unannounced inspections; annual reporting updates required.
    - Extensive regulations on internal controls, accounting, surveillance, security, cage operations, promotions, facility design, responsible gaming, patron exclusion, equipment handling, and junkets.
    - Requirements for minority business participation, employee health and retirement benefits, and local hiring preference (within 10 miles).
    - Transfers/ownership limits: Commission approval/notification for transfers over 5%; automatic revocation after 90 days if buyer not qualified; prohibition on owning interests in more than one video lottery facility; divestiture plans required when seeking additional licenses; good-faith efforts to include minority investors pre- and post-license.
  - Commission may propose changes to the VLT Law that could impact operations.

- New Jersey regulation (Borgata, Atlantic City):
  - Governed by the New Jersey Casino Control Act; oversight by the NJ Casino Control Commission and Division of Gaming Enforcement.
  - NJ Commission issues casino and key employee licenses; NJ Division issues other licenses (including internet gaming and sports wagering) and enforces compliance.
  - Borgata’s casino license renewed effective July 1, 2010 and became indefinite; continuing qualification reviews approximately every five years; license can be reopened at any time (and upon NJ Division request). MGM and subsidiaries qualified as holding companies in September 2014.
  - Qualification requirements extend to officers, directors, beneficial owners, controlling persons, and holding/intermediary/subsidiary entities.
  - Presumption of control at 5%+ equity ownership unless rebutted or waived; institutional investor waivers available under defined circumstances.
  - Financial backers/investors in indebtedness tied to casino operations at 25%+ (or 10% in default) must qualify; others may be required at the NJ Division’s discretion; banks/lending institutions acting in ordinary course are exempt.
  - Restrictions on issuance, ownership, and transfer of a broad range of “securities” of the licensee and its holding/intermediary companies; if a holder is found unqualified, the Commission has authority to act under the NJ Act.

nodes.title: New Jersey Government Regulation
nodes.heading: New Jersey Government Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: Our ownership of Borgata in Atlantic City, New Jersey subjects us to extensive state regulation under the New Jersey Casino Control Act and the regulations promulgated thereunder (collectively, the “NJ Act”) and various other statutes and regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The excerpt details state gaming regulatory frameworks governing the company’s operations in Maryland, New Jersey (Borgata), and Massachusetts (Blue Tarp/MGM Springfield), highlighting licensing, ownership, qualification, and compliance obligations, as well as potential operational impacts of regulatory changes.

- Maryland (VLT Law):
  - Licenses tied to strict regulatory and ownership requirements; failure to meet requirements after a transfer or sale leads to automatic license revocation after 90 days.
  - Prohibition on owning an interest in more than one video lottery facility; applications for additional licenses must include a divestiture plan for the initial interest.
  - Applicants must make serious, good‑faith efforts to solicit and interview minority investors before license award and again for future capital raises.
  - The Maryland Commission can recommend or change VLT regulations, potentially adversely affecting operations.

- New Jersey (Casino Control Act; Borgata):
  - NJ Casino Control Commission and Division of Gaming Enforcement regulate licensing, ownership structures, internet gaming, sports wagering, vendor registrations, and compliance/enforcement.
  - Borgata’s casino license was renewed in 2010 and became indefinite by law, but continuing qualification submissions are required approximately every five years; the Commission can reopen licensing hearings at any time (and must upon the Division’s request). In 2014, certain company entities were qualified as holding companies of Borgata.
  - Broad qualifier requirements: officers, directors, those with control, holding/intermediary/subsidiary entities, and persons holding 5%+ of equity (presumed control unless rebutted or waived). Passive institutional investor waivers are available under defined circumstances.
  - Qualification obligations extend to significant creditors: generally those holding 25%+ of debt (10% in default), with discretion to require others; banks/lenders acting in the ordinary course are exempt.
  - Strict restrictions on issuance, ownership, and transfer of “securities” (equity and certain debt/rights). Disqualified holders can be forced to divest and are barred from exercising rights or receiving economic benefits; non‑divestiture can lead to license suspension or revocation.
  - Corporate charter must require disqualified holders to dispose of securities and allows redemption of such securities by the company.
  - Foreclosure or acquisition of gaming assets requires licensure or interim casino authorization (ICA) before obtaining any ownership interest.

- Massachusetts (Expanded Gaming Act; Blue Tarp/MGM Springfield):
  - Massachusetts Gaming Commission (MGC) issues licenses and ensures suitability; Investigations and Enforcement Bureau (IEB) handles investigations and enforcement, coordinating with State Police and the Attorney General; a Gaming Enforcement Division prosecutes criminal violations.
  - Limited license structure: up to three Category 1 (table games and slots) and one Category 2 (slots only).
  - Blue Tarp and principals were found qualified in 2013; awarded the sole Category 1 license in Region B in 2014. Operations certificate issued September 13, 2018, conditioned on ongoing compliance.
  - License term: 15 years from commencement of operations (August 23, 2018); initial fee of $85 million paid; subject to additional annual fees.
  - Ongoing capital expenditure requirement: generally 3.5% of net gaming revenues annually.
  - Operating parameters: establishments may operate 24/7; patrons must be at least 21; alcohol service restricted during specified early‑morning hours; rules govern check cashing, debit/credit usage, ATMs, and related transactions.

nodes.title: Massachusetts Government Regulation
nodes.heading: Massachusetts Government Regulation
nodes.start_phrase: The Massachusetts Expanded Gaming Act (“Massachusetts Act”) subjects the owners and operators of gaming establishments to extensive state licensing and regulatory requirements.
nodes.summary:
- New Jersey Casino Control Act provisions:
  - Disqualified holders must divest their securities; failure may lead to NJ Commission suspending or revoking related casino licenses.
  - Disqualified holders cannot exercise rights, receive dividends/interest, or be remunerated by affiliated casino licensees.
  - Company charter requires holders found disqualified to dispose of securities and permits the company to redeem such stock.
  - Foreclosure on gaming assets and acquisition of ownership interests require licensure or Interim Casino Authorization (ICA); same applies to prospective purchasers.

- Massachusetts Expanded Gaming Act overview:
  - Massachusetts Gaming Commission (and its Investigations and Enforcement Bureau) oversees licensing, suitability, enforcement, and ongoing regulation; licenses are revocable privileges.
  - Up to three Category 1 (tables and slots) and one Category 2 (slots only) licenses statewide.

- Blue Tarp reDevelopment, LLC (Springfield, MA) specifics:
  - Found qualified on December 23, 2013; awarded the sole Category 1 Region B license on November 6, 2014 (effective November 7, 2014).
  - Operations certificate issued September 13, 2018; license term is 15 years commencing August 23, 2018.
  - Paid $85,000,000 initial license fee; subject to annual fees and a continuing capital expenditure requirement equal to at least 3.5% of net gaming revenues.

- Operating and transactional rules:
  - Establishments may operate 24/7; patrons must be 21+; alcohol service restricted during specified early-morning hours inside/outside the gaming area.
  - Regulations govern check cashing, debit/credit card use, and ATMs.

- Suitability, compliance, and enforcement:
  - Background investigations and qualifications required for applicants, affiliates, executives, employees, financiers, debt holders, and persons/entities with 5%+ interests (with possible institutional investor exemptions).
  - Ongoing oversight includes fee collection, inspections, monitoring, investigations, and civil penalties; licenses can be suspended, revoked, or conditioned for violations.

- Detailed regulatory requirements include:
  - Employee and vendor licensing/registration; accounting/internal controls; surveillance/security; device/system registration and testing; self-exclusion.
  - Reporting and approvals for construction and operations; temporary licensure; marketing and affirmative marketing plans.
  - Notifications/approvals for changes in shareholders, executives, qualifiers, and material events/transactions.
  - Complimentary services; political contributions; credit issuance and customer transactions; auditing/record retention.
  - Facility design and floor plans; slot possession/transport; table game procedures; employee credentials; vendors/junkets; count room/cage procedures.

- Ownership and control restrictions:
  - Transfers of interests or licenses require Commission notification and approval; security transfers are ineffective if disapproved.
  - Changes to governing structure require approval; cross-ownership of another licensee’s license or establishment is prohibited.

- Regulatory flexibility:
  - Commission may promulgate, amend, or repeal regulations, which could affect operations; some rules remain in draft form.

nodes.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated financial statements of CityCenter Holdings, LLC and its subsidiaries (the “Company”), which comprise the consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2018 and 2017, and the related consolidated statements of operations, members’ equity, and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2018, and the related notes to the consolidated financial statements.
nodes.summary:
- Independent Auditors’ Report by Deloitte & Touche LLP on CityCenter Holdings, LLC and subsidiaries’ consolidated financial statements.
- Scope: Audits of consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2018 and 2017, and consolidated statements of operations, members’ equity, and cash flows for each of the three years ended December 31, 2018, including related notes.
- Management’s responsibility: Preparation and fair presentation under U.S. GAAP and maintenance of relevant internal controls.
- Auditors’ responsibility: Conducted under U.S. GAAS; risk assessment and consideration of internal control for planning purposes only; no opinion on internal control effectiveness; evaluation of accounting policies, estimates, and presentation; sufficient appropriate audit evidence obtained.
- Opinion: Unmodified—financial position, results of operations, and cash flows are fairly presented in all material respects under U.S. GAAP.
- Emphasis of Matter: Adoption of FASB ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) effective January 1, 2018, on a full retrospective basis; opinion not modified.

nodes.title: BASIS OF PRESENTATION AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.heading: NOTE 2 — BASIS OF PRESENTATION AND SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.start_phrase: The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Company and its subsidiaries.
nodes.summary:
- Organization and governance: CityCenter Holdings, LLC is a 50/50 Delaware joint venture between MGM Resorts International and Infinity World (Dubai World). It has a six-member board (three appointed by each member), no employees, and relies on MGM Resorts under management agreements to operate CityCenter.

- Nature of business and properties: CityCenter is a mixed-use complex on the Las Vegas Strip including Aria Resort & Casino, Vdara Hotel & Spa, and Veer Towers (all condo units sold by 2016). The Company sold Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas in August 2018 and The Shops at Crystals in April 2016.

- Basis of presentation: Consolidated financial statements of the Company and its subsidiaries with elimination of intercompany items; no involvement with variable interest entities; results not necessarily indicative of future performance.

- Key accounting policies and estimates:
  - Use of estimates affecting reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses.
  - Fair value measurements framework (Levels 1–3); Level 2 used for interest rate swaps recognized in other assets or other long-term obligations.
  - Cash equivalents defined as investments with maturities of 90 days or less.
  - Accounts receivable and credit risk: issuance of casino markers, significant foreign customer exposure (about half of casino receivables), allowance for doubtful accounts based on specific review and history.
  - Inventories at lower of cost or market; average cost for F&B and supplies; cost method for retail.
  - Residential real estate accounting (last units sold in 2016).
  - Property and equipment: capitalization policies, useful lives, accrued construction payables/retentions, and gains/losses on disposals.
  - Project changes: closure of Zarkana theater to expand convention space, resulting in accelerated depreciation in 2016; convention expansion opened Q1 2018.
  - Capitalized interest during development; impairment testing for long-lived assets held-and-used.
  - Other assets include indefinite-lived intangibles tested annually with no impairments recorded.
  - Debt issuance costs capitalized and amortized to interest expense.

- Revenue recognition (ASC 606):
  - Casino revenue recognized as net win; discounts on markers reduce casino revenue.
  - Allocation of casino transaction price to complimentary goods/services and loyalty incentives based on standalone selling price (with breakage estimates); third-party comps expensed.
  - Non-casino revenue (rooms, food and beverage, entertainment, retail) recognized upon transfer of goods/services; agent vs. principal presentation assessed for certain arrangements (e.g., OTAs, some shows).
  - Bundled arrangements allocated by relative standalone selling prices.
  - Contract and related liabilities include outstanding chips, loyalty program obligations, and customer advances/front money; generally recognized as revenue within one year.
  - Lease income from third parties presented within the related revenue categories.

- Other policies: Real estate sales recognized at closing when criteria met; advertising expensed when first run (with disclosed annual amounts); property transactions, net, used for asset-related gains/losses; no income tax provision as the entity is a partnership; comprehensive income equals net income; prior-period reclassifications for comparability.

- Recently issued/adopted standards:
  - ASC 606 adopted retrospectively effective January 1, 2018, resulting in:
    - Elimination of a separate promotional allowances revenue offset line; reallocations among revenue categories.
    - Loyalty liability recognized at retail value (less breakage), with an initial retained earnings decrease and offset to due to MGM Resorts.
    - Certain items (e.g., F&B service charges, wide area progressive fees) presented gross.
    - Ceased reclassifying estimated costs of complimentaries among expense lines.
    - Overall immaterial impact on net income and cash flows; quantified reclassifications provided for 2017 and 2016.
  - ASC 842 Leases to be adopted January 1, 2019 with right-of-use assets and lease liabilities recognized; practical expedients elected; no recast of prior periods.
  - ASU 2016-15 (cash flow classification) adopted with no material effect.
  - Subsequent events evaluated through February 19, 2019.

- Assets held for sale and discontinued operations:
  - Mandarin Oriental sold in August 2018 for approximately $214 million, resulting in a $133 million loss recorded in discontinued operations; its results presented as discontinued operations for 2018, 2017, and 2016; assets and liabilities classified as held for sale at December 31, 2017.
  - The Shops at Crystals sold in April 2016 for approximately $1.1 billion, resulting in a $400 million gain in discontinued operations; results presented as discontinued operations for 2016.
  - Disclosures include components of assets held for sale/liabilities and notes on capital expenditures and cash flow presentation related to discontinued operations.
